activity: to compare two apartment leases and work out the total monthly cost including utilities
knowledge_domain: to compare two apartment leases and work out the total monthly cost including utilities
fact: Ontario requires most private residential landlords to use a government standard lease form for new leases, and a tenant can request one in writing if it was not provided.
story:
I should say up front that I am good with numbers, and that this has been the one thing about me I never doubted. My mother's nickname for me is Calculator. So when she pushed two leases across the kitchen table on Sunday night and said, "You pick, we'll sign whichever you can actually afford," I felt something in my chest go quiet and sure, the way it does before a test I'm going to destroy.

The first lease was for a basement apartment on Carlaw, $1,350 a month, all utilities included, from a landlord named Mr. Ma. The second was a one-bedroom above a hardware store, $1,290, plus hydro, plus water heating, plus something called a "utility disbursement" that the lease said the tenant reimbursed monthly, which I took to mean I would be paying out money to the landlord for things I couldn't see or measure. I made two columns. I estimated hydro at ninety dollars in a bad month. I felt very adult.

I called Tina, because Tina had moved out in March and had opinions the way other people have furniture. "Which one," I said, holding the phone with my shoulder while I added a column for internet.

"The Carlaw one, obviously," she said. "Cheaper once you count everything. Also my cousin's friend lives on that street and says it's fine."

"Fine is not data," I said, and she laughed at me, and I wrote 1,350 in the Carlaw column and underlined it twice. That is the version of the call I told my mother about later. The truth, which I only admitted to myself while brushing my teeth that night, is that I had already decided before I called her. The columns came after the decision. They underpinned it, technically. They were also decoration.

The problem surfaced on Tuesday, in the fine print, where I was looking for parking. The Carlaw lease, the one I wanted, was fourteen pages of clauses in Mr. Ma's own wording, no visitor policy, an obdurate little paragraph about "quiet enjoyment at the discretion of the landlord," which is not a thing, and I knew it was not a thing because August had spent all of April ranting about tenant rights after his building tried to ban his girlfriend from the lobby. The hardware store lease, by contrast, was twelve pages of an official-looking form with a government header, boxes, prescribed wording. One of these was the real standard lease that Ontario makes landlords use, and it wasn't the one I'd picked.

I texted August instead of looking it up myself, which is a habit I'm not proud of. He called back within a minute, breathless from a run. "Yeah, for most private residential places, new leases have to be on the government's standard form. That's the one with the header. If you didn't get one, you can ask for it in writing and they have to give it to you."

"In writing," I repeated, scribbling on the back of an envelope.

"That's what the thing says. A letter, an email, something on record."

So here is what I did, and here is where I have to be honest about my own motives, because my mother got a version of this too. I wrote Mr. Ma an email that was polite in a way that felt like handling glass. I said I was interested in the apartment. I said that I noticed the lease wasn't on the standard form, and that I was requesting one in writing, and that I understood a tenant could do that. I read it four times. I did not mention the hardware store lease, or the columns, or the fact that I had already told Tina and half my group chat that I'd found my apartment. Sent, 9:47 p.m.

He replied at 6:10 the next morning, which told me something about him before a single word did. "Of course," he wrote. "I have the standard form ready. Sign whichever you prefer, they say the same thing." And then, attached, twelve pages with the government header, and a note: "Utilities included, as discussed. Total is the total."

They did not say the same thing. That was the twist, though it felt less like a twist and more like a door opening onto a room I'd been standing outside of while insisting I knew its layout. The standard version had no quiet enjoyment clause at the landlord's discretion, no visitor policy, and the included utilities were spelled out line by line, kilowatt by kilowatt, so that the number I'd underlined twice turned out to be the actual number. The hardware store lease, the official one, the one that had made me feel safe, put hydro on me and that disbursement on me and, buried in a box I'd skimmed, an eighty-dollar locker fee I had never counted.

I sat at the kitchen table with all three documents fanned out, my columns obsolete, my sureness gone, and for once I didn't mind that it was gone. My mother came in and put a hand on my shoulder.

"Which one?" she said.

"I'm writing Mr. Ma back," I said, and pulled the laptop toward me.

activity: to plan a weekly training program for a sport with rest days and warm-ups
knowledge_domain: to plan a weekly training program for a sport with rest days and warm-ups
fact: In a 2011 Stanford study, basketball players who aimed for 10 hours in bed nightly improved their free-throw average from 7.9 to 8.8 successful shots out of 10.
story:
Maxime arrived at the community pool at six in the morning with a spiral notebook, a pencil sharpened to a needle, and a plan he had spent half the night proving wrong. He had written out a weekly training program for the fall triathlon club, seven days of drills, and then, somewhere around one in the morning, he had crossed out every Saturday entry and written REST in capitals so aggressive the paper tore. Now he stood at the chain-link gate watching Mr. Campbell fiddle with the lock, and the torn page flapped against his thigh.

"You're early," Mr. Campbell said. "Or late from last night. Hard to tell with you."

"Early," Maxime said. "Definitely early."

Rhiannon was already inside, doing warm-up laps without being asked, which was her way of announcing she intended to be club captain and had already begun, in her head, the campaign. She wanted the position the way other people wanted concert tickets: quietly, constantly, and with a spreadsheet. When Maxime set his notebook on the bench, she appeared at the edge of the water like a small ambitious seal.

"Is that the training plan? Can I see it?"

"It's a draft." He hesitated, then turned it toward her, because keeping it hidden would cost more than showing it. Rhiannon read the way she swam, fast and without wasted motion.

"Rest day, good. Warm-up protocol, good. Then why do you look like your dog died?"

Rayna hauled herself out of the far lane, wrapped a towel around her shoulders, and came over, dripping on the notebook, which she did not apologize for because she never apologized for anything and everyone had agreed, years ago, to find it charming. "He looks like that because he stayed up until two making a plan about not staying up late," she said. "I watched him do it. We were messaging. He was very morose around one-thirty. He used the word futile."

"Twice," Maxime admitted.

Rhiannon sat down on the bench, pulling her knees up, which meant she was about to be reasonable at him. "So the plan has rest days for us and none for you."

"That's not," he began, and then stopped, because it was exactly that. He had spent the summer reading everything he could find about training, and one thing had lodged in him like a splinter. A 2011 Stanford study, he'd found it on the fourth page of search results one night. Basketball players who aimed for ten hours in bed every night improved their free-throw average from 7.9 successful shots out of 10 to 8.8. He had underlined it twice. He had then gone to bed at two in the morning, and the next night, and the next, as though the fact were a patrimony he could inherit without ever collecting it.

"Here's my problem," he said, and it came out steadier than he felt. "I know rest is part of training. The research is real, it's not guesswork. Basketball players, Stanford, 2011. Ten hours in bed, and their free throws went from 7.9 to 8.8 out of 10. That's a whole extra make per ten shots, just from lying in bed. But knowing it and doing it are two different sports." He tapped the notebook. "So I planned everyone else's sleep like it was a drill, and treated mine as optional. Which is a weird way to respect a fact."

Rayna wrung out her ponytail, considering. "So what's the fix? You sequester your phone in the kitchen at ten? My mom does that. She calls it the charging station like it's a tiny prison."

"Something like that," Maxime said. "I don't know yet if it works. That's the honest version. I can write warm-ups into the plan and count on them. I can't count on me."

Rhiannon stood, and for a second he thought she was going to make it about the captaincy, some speech about leaders modeling behavior, but instead she said, "Then don't count on you. Count on us. Give me the draft. I'll put the whole week on the club board, your name at the top, ten hours in bed for everyone, you included. Public plan. You fail, we all see it." She smiled without malice. "Also I've wanted to run a board since grade ten, so this is a good day for me."

"That's blackmail with a whiteboard," Maxime said.

"It's governance."

Mr. Campbell, who had finished unlocking and had been listening from the shallow end with the deep patience of a man paid slightly too little, called out that if the parliament would like to swim, lane one was open. Rayna cannonballed before anyone could object, and Rhiannon dove in clean, and Maxime stood a moment longer at the bench, pencil hovering over the torn page. Then he wrote his own name at the top of the sleep column, alongside everyone else's, and set the pencil down.

"Lane four," he said to himself, and jumped.

activity: to temper chocolate so it sets shiny and snaps cleanly
knowledge_domain: to temper chocolate so it sets shiny and snaps cleanly
fact: Form V cocoa butter crystals melt at about 33.8 degrees Celsius, just below body temperature, which is why well-tempered chocolate melts in the mouth but not in the hand.
story:
I am not a person who dwells on things, which is why I can tell you exactly how the farmers' market went wrong, and why I had stopped thinking about it by Tuesday. Mr. Lau's cooking class had a unit on chocolate, and I wanted ours to be the table people remembered. That is all. There was nothing morose about me that week, whatever Kennedy says, and I only checked the thermometer eleven times because precision matters when you are tempering.

Tempering is the part nobody appreciates. You melt the chocolate hot, cool it while you stir, and warm it again just slightly, all to coax the cocoa butter into the right crystal structure. Mr. Lau had handed out thermometers and a scrap of paper with temperatures written on it, but he refused to explain the theory. "You'll figure out why," he said, "or you won't." So I stirred. Kareem, at the next station, had already ruined two batches and gone morose over them, holding his bowl like something that had died. Mine glossed over smooth and quiet when I spread a test smear on parchment, and when it set, it snapped. A clean, glassy crack.

The problem, if there was one, started at the market. Kennedy and I ran the table together, chocolate bark in paper trays, the whole point being to sell enough to fund the class's spring dinner. October sun on the tables, and our chocolate sat there solid hour after hour, while the woman selling fudge two stalls down kept apologizing for hers going soft. Kareem wandered over on his break and took a piece without paying, which I noted and forgave, and held it in his fist while he argued with Kennedy about something. When he finally ate it, he stopped mid-sentence.

"Wait," he said. "It was solid in my hand. Like actually solid, the whole time. And now it's just gone." He looked at his palm, then at his tongue, as though one of them had betrayed him. "It's melted all at once."

 Kennedy's version, written later in a message she sent me that night, went like this: "You said it was luck. You said, and I quote, 'the weather was lucky.' You dichotomize everything into luck or skill, and when it's your skill you call it luck, which is a weird kind of litotes, like saying your chocolate was 'not bad.' It wasn't not bad. It was the best thing at the market." She had sent it at one in the morning, which I know because I was awake, not dwelling, just awake, and I read it four times. "Also," the message went on, "you never once told anyone how you did it. People asked. The fudge lady asked. You smiled and said practice. That's not an answer, Alicia."

Here is what I actually knew, and what I hadn't told anyone. On Thursday, cleaning up while everyone else had left, I had found Mr. Lau's actual notes face down by the sink, and on them a line about the crystals in tempered chocolate. Form V, the notes called them, the form that mattered. Form V cocoa butter crystals melt at about 33.8 degrees Celsius, just below body temperature. That was why. Why our chocolate had sat solid on the table all afternoon, unmoved by the October sun, and had vanished the instant it touched a tongue. I had read it twice, put the paper back, and stirred my batch with my heart going strangely fast, as though I'd been given something meant for someone further along than me. Whether Mr. Lau left it there on purpose, I still don't know. He said nothing about it, then or since, and I have not asked.

So when people at the market asked how, and I said practice, it was not entirely a lie. I had practiced. But I had also been given, or had found, or had stolen, the reason, and saying "practice" let me keep both: the credit for the work and the secret of the knowledge. Kennedy, who dichotomizes nothing, who would have told the fudge lady everything, saw that plainly enough to write it down at one in the morning.

In class on Wednesday Mr. Lau had us temper again, second round. Kareem was still on his first attempt, morose again, bent over his bowl, and Kennedy kept glancing at me in the way that meant she wanted an answer more than an apology. My chocolate came to temperature and I spread the test smear, watched it set, snapped it clean between my fingers. Then I picked up the piece and held it in my closed hand for a long moment, feeling it hold, feeling the edge of warmth against my skin, and walked it over to Kareem's station.

"Form V," I said, and put it on his tongue.

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: In mayonnaise, lecithin and proteins from egg yolk act as emulsifiers, holding tiny oil droplets suspended in water so the sauce does not separate.
story:
Dominic stood at the steel counter of the community kitchen with three eggs, a bottle of neutral oil, and a whisk, and the clock on the wall said four-forty. His mother's shift ended at six, his father was already on his second job, and his little sister expected dinner, not an apology. He had signed up for the Thursday cooking slot because it was free and because Ms. Ross, who ran the place, had said anyone could use the pantry staples if they replaced what they took. Tonight he was making chicken and a potato salad, and the potato salad required mayonnaise, and Ms. Ross had looked at him when he reached for the jar on the shelf and said, "You have eggs. Make it."

The first attempt went wrong in the way that things go wrong when you are confident. He dropped the oil in too fast, all at once, thinking a whisk could fix speed. The mixture turned thin and greasy, then separated entirely into a pool of oil sitting on top of a sad yellowish liquid. He stood over it with his hands on the counter. Behind him, two men he didn't know were chopping onions for the shelter's evening meal, and a radio pundit was going on about the city budget, querulous and relentless, and Dominic could not tell which noise irritated him more.

Antonia came in with her backpack still on one shoulder. She worked the dessert station on Thursdays, and she paused when she saw the bowl. "That's not mayonnaise," she said.

"It's mayonnaise in theory. It's oil and water in practice."

She leaned over the bowl and poked at the surface with a spoon. "My grandmother would say you rushed it. She'd also say something about the moon, so you can't trust everything she says." Antonia pulled out her phone, scrolled, and held up a page. "Look, there's a whole rescue method. My nonna does it without looking anything up."

Dominic read the screen. The words told him what he had actually been doing, which was suspending tiny oil droplets in water, held apart and held together by the lecithin and proteins in egg yolk. Those were the emulsifiers, the page said, the things that kept the sauce from separating. He had been treating the yolk like an ingredient, one item on a list, when it was the entire structure. Drop the oil too fast and the droplets merged, the structure collapsed, and the sauce broke into its two selves.

"You need a fresh yolk," Antonia said. "Separate it into a clean bowl. Then you whisk the broken stuff into it, slowly, like you should have done the first time."

He separated the egg one-handed, badly, and fished out a scrap of shell. He put the new yolk in a clean bowl and added a teaspoon of the ruined liquid, whisking until it turned smooth and opaque. Then another teaspoon. The science said the new yolk would gather the old droplets and hold them again, and he had two choices with this information: believe it or drive to the store and buy the jar. His mother had a phrase for people who quit at the interesting part, and she never said it kindly.

He poured a thin stream of oil, whisking, and the sauce tightened around the whisk. It thickened, went pale, took on the gloss of something that had been burnished rather than merely mixed. He tasted it. It tasted like mayonnaise, which felt like a small and unreasonable victory.

Francesco came over from the pasta station to watch the last minute of it. "So it broke and you fixed it with another yolk," he said. "That's it?"

"That's it, but it's not nothing. The whole thing exists because of what's in the yolk. I was thinking of it like a recipe, like steps you follow. It's more like a structure you build and can also rebuild."

Francesco shrugged and went back to his pasta, and Dominic did not blame him. A month ago he would have shrugged too. He had been arguing with his father all summer about college, his father saying a business degree was a safe structure and Dominic saying he wanted engineering, and neither of them had known what they were actually arguing about. Tonight, whisking, he understood that he had been treating the argument like a recipe, a fixed set of steps with one correct outcome, when his father was really asking whether the thing Dominic wanted would hold together under pressure. That was a fair question. He didn't have the answer yet, only the beginnings of one: the answer was neither the safe jar on the shelf nor the fantasy of never breaking. It was knowing what held things together and being willing to do the slow work when they came apart.

He plated the potato salad and wrapped the chicken for the walk home. Antonia rinsed the bowl he had ruined, without being asked, and set it upside down to dry.

"You're smiling at a bowl," she said.

"I'm smiling at the second bowl."

"Take some eggs home," Ms. Ross said from the pantry door. "You'll break it again."

He took six, put them in his backpack wrapped in a dish towel, and went out into the early dark with the food warm against his side.

activity: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
knowledge_domain: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
fact: Using 2007 survey data, the US Census Bureau estimated that a person in the United States can expect to move about 11.7 times in a lifetime.
story:
The last box went into the trunk at six in the morning, and by seven Hannah was in the back seat with her knees against the seat in front of her because the boxes from her closet had claimed the rest. Her father drove. Her mother rode shotgun with the atlas folded on her lap even though the phone was giving directions anyway, because she liked to see the whole route at once, liked knowing where the rivers were.

They were three hours from the old house and two hours from the new one when her mother turned around in her seat. "You know we're not unusual," she said. "I looked it up last night. Using 2007 survey data, the US Census Bureau estimated that a person in the United States can expect to move about 11.7 times in a lifetime."

"Eleven point seven," Hannah said.

"About. On average." Her mother said it gently, the way she'd say it's supposed to rain, but Hannah heard the argument underneath: everyone does this, so stop treating it like a catastrophe. Except averages weren't lives. Some people never left the street they were born on, which meant other people were doing all the moving for them, somewhere, in some other back seat.

Her phone buzzed against her thigh. Toby had sent a photo of the parking spot behind the gym where they used to sit after track practice, the one with the crack shaped like a lightning bolt, and underneath it: "they're paving it today. Tania says hi. She says it's your fault." Three hearts after that, so it was a joke, but Hannah held the phone against her sternum for a while before answering.

Toby had tried to cajole her into skipping the last week of school, promising they'd drive to the lake and she could say goodbye to the water instead of to a building. She'd refused, and now she was glad and sorry at once, because the goodbyes had been terrible and the lake would have been worse. In biology they'd spent the spring on the immune system, and her notebook from that class was in the box under her feet. She'd written in the margin, in her own handwriting, that an antigen was anything the body decided was foreign, anything it chose to react against, and Toby had read it over her shoulder and said, "So basically anything new is an attack." He'd meant it as a joke about the unit test. She thought about it now.

"Eleven point seven," her father said from the front, catching the tail of her thinking. "I've done nine. Nine in fifty-one years." He drummed the wheel. "So either I've got two point seven left in me, or I'm done, and somebody else is picking up my slack." He glanced at her in the mirror. "You've got one. You've got ten point seven to go. That's not an ending, that's inventory."

It was a ridiculous kind of comfort, and it worked anyway, a little. She had spent the whole summer holding two ideas that wouldn't sit in the same pocket: that leaving was a real loss, that Tania's particular laugh and Toby's habit of saving her the seat closest to the door could not be replaced, and that she would in fact be fine, would probably in some ways be more herself in a place where no one had already decided who she was. For weeks she'd treated those ideas as opponents. In the car, watching the guardrail stutter past, she let them sit side by side instead. Both could be true. The loss didn't cancel the fine, and the fine didn't make the loss smaller. What stayed uncertain was whether ten point seven more moves would make her practiced at this or just tired of it, and she understood that no one could tell her that in advance, not even the Census Bureau.

Tania had given her a length of copper wire at the going-away party, coiled into a loose spiral, because in physics Tania had been delighted to learn that copper was ductile, that you could pull it and it would stretch thin without snapping, and she'd said, "That's us, don't forget," which was embarrassing and which Hannah had not thrown out. The wire was in her backpack on the seat beside her, along with her phone, which buzzed again. Toby: "paving guys say the crack will still be under there. somewhere."

Hannah pulled the spiral of wire out and held it in the light from the window, then stretched it gently between her hands, feeling where it wanted to bend. "Dad," she said, "when we stop for gas, can I get a postcard? The really ugly kind." "The uglier the better," he said, and turned off at the exit.

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: The Hindu festival of Holi falls on the full moon of the month Phalguna, usually in March, and begins with a bonfire the night before called Holika Dahan.
story:
The bonfire had been stacked since noon, a wooden tower taller than Jeremy's uncle, and Jeremy had been assigned to guard it from the neighborhood kids who kept trying to steal branches for their own smaller, rival fire two streets over. He sat on an upturned crate with a thermos of chai and his phone at eleven percent, because he had promised Renee and Kareem he would meet them at the arcade by eight, and it was already seven fifteen.

"You're on duty," his mother had said, gesticulating at the pile with a wooden spoon as though the wood might bolt if unwatched. "The whole family is on duty. It's Holi, beta. You can play games any Tuesday."

It was, in fact, not a Tuesday, and Jeremy had checked, which he felt was a point in his favor. He had also looked up why everyone was so particular about tonight, because nobody at home explained things, they just expected you to absorb them like a sponge left in a sink. What he found was this: the festival fell on the full moon of the month Phalguna, usually in March, and it began the night before with a bonfire. He'd texted the word to Kareem, who had replied "bless you."

At seven thirty his cousin Priya arrived, though at family gatherings she was introduced only as "your cousin," and behind her came Renee, holding a paper bag of marshmallows as an offering.

"You brought marshmallows to a religious fire," Jeremy said.

"I brought marshmallows to a fire. The fire doesn't have a religion, it's on fire." Renee looked up at the wood tower, then at the moon rising fat and white over the rooftops. "Is that the actual full moon? Like the real one?"

"That's the one. It's the whole reason tonight is tonight." He pointed at the moon with his thermos. "Holi's on the full moon of Phalguna. Usually March. And the night before, you do this."

"Do what, specifically, guard it?"

"Ha ha. The bonfire. It's called Holika Dahan," said Priya, in the tone of someone reciting something she had been quizzed on annually since the age of six. "Dahan means burning, before you ask."

Renee, to her credit, did not ask, and instead attempted to roast a marshmallow over a candle someone had set near the crate for no reason anyone could defend. The marshmallow caught fire and she waved the stick around with such enthusiasm that Priya had to relocate a small antiquity, a brass lamp older than everyone present, to a safer step.

At eight the uncle arrived with matches and a look of phlegmatic calm that suggested he had done this forty times and had seen fires misbehave in every available way. But the tower caught cleanly, flames climbing the stacked branches, and the neighbors came out, and someone put on music, and Priya's little brother tried to throw his own shoe into the fire and was intercepted mid-throw like a goalkeeper's save.

Jeremy had meant to leave at eight. He had it planned: five minutes of fire, polite exit, arcade by eight forty. Instead he found himself third in line to walk around the flames, Renee beside him, still holding her marshmallow stick like a torch, and when his mother offered him a second cup of chai he took it without calculating the time cost at all, which for him was roughly the equivalent of scaling a mountain barefoot.

Around nine, Kareem appeared, out of breath, having walked from the arcade. "You stood us up," he said.

"You could have come here," Jeremy said. "I told you about it."

"You said 'Holi thing,' which sounded like a thing with aunts."

"There are aunts. There's also a giant fire."

Kareem looked at the fire, and at Priya demonstrating the correct technique for throwing roasted grain into the flames, which was mostly in the wrist, and at the full moon sitting exactly where it was supposed to be, presiding over the whole arrangement like a supervisor who had approved the paperwork. He took off his jacket.

"Fine," he said. "But tomorrow, when everyone's throwing color at everyone, I'm getting you first. Full bucket. I've already chosen the bucket."

"You'll have to catch me," Jeremy said, and Kareem, solemnly, shook his hand on it.

activity: to apply a feminist or Marxist critical lens to a passage from a classic novel
knowledge_domain: to apply a feminist or Marxist critical lens to a passage from a classic novel
fact: Charlotte Brontë first published Jane Eyre in 1847 under the name Currer Bell, which did not reveal that its author was a woman.
story:
The bookshop on Mercer Street kept its classics in the back room, where the ceiling lamps buzzed and the secondhand copies smelled faintly of someone else's attic. Nolan had come in for a cheap copy of Jane Eyre, which Mr. Pritchard's English seminar required by Monday, and he found one with a cracked spine and a yellowed title page. He was checking the price penciled inside the cover when Olivier elbowed past him toward the poetry shelf.

"Find it?" Olivier asked, holding a slim volume of his own.

"Five dollars. But look at this." Nolan turned the book so Olivier could see the title page. The author's name printed there was not Brontë at all. It read, in faded serif type, Currer Bell.

"That's not the author," Olivier said.

"It says it right here." Nolan flipped the pages, as if the explanation might be tucked between them. "Currer Bell. Nothing about a Charlotte anywhere in the front matter."

Vivian arrived from the front counter with a stack of Norton anthologies she was supposedly reshelving. She took the book from Nolan, read the title page, and looked at him with the particular patience she reserved for things she thought he should already know. "Charlotte Brontë first published Jane Eyre in 1847 under the name Currer Bell," she said. "It didn't reveal that its author was a woman."

Nolan stared at the page. "Why not?"

"Why do you think."

He thought about it while she and Olivier argued over whether the shop's space heater was a fire hazard. The name was a mask, but calling it a mask wasn't enough; a mask implied a face underneath that stayed the same, and he wasn't sure that was true. If the book had to arrive in the world as a man's work in order to be read at all, then something about the book itself, how it could move, where it could go, had been shaped by the mask before a single reader opened it. He tried to say this out loud and it came out clunky, something about the pseudonym being part of the architecture rather than the wallpaper.

"That's actually not bad," Vivian said. "Pritchard would call that a feminist lens. You're reading the conditions of production, not just the plot."

"Which is more than I'm doing," Olivier said, "since I still haven't finished the poetry unit."

They took over the small table by the window, the one with the coffee rings, and Vivian made Nolan work. She opened her own copy to the early chapters and told him to read the passage where young Jane is locked in the red-room, then say something. He read it twice. The first time he narrated the plot back to her, and she shook her head. The second time he noticed that the red-room was the room of a dead man, that Jane was being punished inside the physical remains of male authority, that the punishment was for defiance. The room reified the power Jane had offended against; it took something abstract, the uncle's dominance, and made it walls and a locked door and a cold bed. Vivian tapped the table.

"Good. Now the other one. Pritchard wants both, doesn't he?"

Nolan found the passage where Jane is sent to Lowood, and the cold porridge, and Mr. Brocklehurst preaching humility while his own daughters stand in silk and fur. He read it aloud in a flat voice, because the flatness seemed right. The girls were being trained for a labor market that would pay them almost nothing, and the charity that fed them was the same machinery that kept them cheap. Brocklehurst's sermon about plainness was pithy in the worst way, a compact little sentence that dressed poverty up as virtue so nobody had to fix it. He said the school was a synecdoche for something larger, the part standing in for the whole system, and Vivian wrote the word down on the back of her hand.

"Which lens do you actually believe?" Olivier asked. He had given up on poetry and was watching them over the rim of the window. "You can't do both. Either it's about gender or it's about money."

Nolan looked at the old title page again, at Currer Bell printed there like a fact of nature. He thought that the two readings kept colliding and kept needing each other. Jane was poor because she was a woman without family, and she was a woman without family in a world where that condition made her poor; the pseudonym sat exactly where the two explanations crossed. He could not separate them without making one of them smaller. But he also knew he hadn't finished the novel, and that a reading built on two hundred pages was a reading built on sand, and that Mr. Pritchard would ask on Monday what he was still unsure about and he would have to say so out loud.

"Both," he said. "And I don't know yet how the ending changes it. Ask me after I read the last chapter."

Vivian closed her anthology, stood, and carried the stack she had abandoned back toward the shelves. Then she stopped, turned, and held out her hand for the five dollars.

"If we're buying the evidence," she said, "I want to see that title page again on Monday."

activity: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
knowledge_domain: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
fact: In 1896, Swedish scientist Svante Arrhenius made the first calculation of how much Earth would warm if the amount of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere doubled.
story:
The quarry had filled with rainwater years ago, and the town called it the Blue Hole now, though Sofia thought of it as a wound that had learned to be beautiful. She spread her notes on a flat slab of limestone near the edge, where Guneet and Josue were already sitting, and opened her notebook to the graph she had copied twice and still did not trust.

"Quizzing me," she said. "For real. Not the nice version."

Mr. Rahimi had offered her the make-up presentation because she had frozen during the climate unit, and she had frozen because her father worked at the plant off Route 9, and half the town's paychecks came out of the ground one way or another. She had not been able to make her mouth explain the graph. Mr. Rahimi had only said, "Take the weekend. Explain it somewhere that helps you think." So she had chosen the quarry, because it was where the Earth had been cut open and you could see the layers, older and older the farther down you looked.

Guneet held up the graph, the Keeling curve, the line climbing from the lower left like a road out of the pit. "Okay. Why does it climb after 1950?"

"Because carbon dioxide traps outgoing heat. Sunlight comes in as visible light, the Earth warms, and it radiates infrared back out. The molecules absorb the infrared and re-emit it, some of it downward, so the surface stays warmer than it would." She said it steadily, and Josue, who had been skipping stones with an insouciant flick of the wrist that made it look easy when it was not, stopped and turned around.

"Wait," he said. "Say the trapping part again. Slower."

She said it again, slower, and then made him say it back, and then made Guneet do the same, and then took the graph and asked them to point to where the slope steepened. Guneet found it, the sharp bend after mid-century. Josue ran his finger along the decades and asked the question Sofia had been half dreading, the one that always sounded like an escape hatch: "But how do we know? This is all models, right? Computers didn't even exist back when."

Sofia took out her phone, and after a moment of searching she found it and read aloud. "In 1896, the Swedish scientist Svante Arrhenius made the first calculation of how much Earth would warm if the amount of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere doubled." She looked up. "Eighteen ninety-six. No computers. He did it by hand."

The wind moved across the water and the boys were quiet, and Sofia felt the two halves of her life sit down next to each other on the stone. Half of her wanted the whole thing to be wrong, or at least unproven, because her father's job was warm and lit and real, and a graph was a graph. The other half knew that wanting something did not make it false, and that the two loyalties were not actually opposites, they just felt like it. She had been treating the science as a threat to her family instead of as information her family deserved to have, honestly given, by someone who loved them.

"I'm going to text my dad," she said. "Before Monday."

She typed it leaning over the graph so he could see the photo of it: Found out the first estimate of warming from doubled CO2 was calculated in 1896, by hand, by a Swedish scientist named Arrhenius. Before computers. I know this is complicated for us. I'm not trying to fight about it. I just want to be the one who tells you, not some stranger.

The reply came while Josue was showing Guneet the trick with the wrist, the angle that made the stone count five instead of two. Her father wrote, Cold out there? and then, a minute later, longer: Not a fight. Bring the graph home, I want to see the part where it bends. Ask your teacher if the plant's numbers are in there.

Sofa read it twice, then folded the phone closed against her palm. There were things she still could not answer, like how much of the steepening slope had her street's name on it, and whether her father would look at the graph the same way once he did see it, and what she would say on Monday when someone in class asked the question Josue had asked and she had to stand there without her notes.

She picked up a flat stone, weighed it, and walked to the edge.

"Watch the wrist," Josue said. "It's all in the wrist."

She threw, and the stone skipped once, twice, and on the third skip Guneet shouted the count into the quarry air.

activity: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
knowledge_domain: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
fact: Psychologist John Gottman distinguishes a complaint, which addresses a specific behavior, from criticism, which attacks the person's character.
story:
The bleachers by the far field were still wet from the morning rain, so Eli sat on his bag and watched Boston run the drill again, alone, after everyone else had gone to the water jugs. Boston had fumbled the pass three times in a row, and the third time he had shouted at himself, loud enough that Mr. Robinson paused his stopwatch and looked over.

"You're not watching the ball into your hands," Eli called out.

Boston jogged to the fence, breathing hard. "Thanks, Coach," he said, petulant, though he was the one who had asked for help. "I know that. I know what I'm doing wrong. That's not the problem."

Eeli had been sent over by Mr. Robinson, who had said only, "Tell him what you see, Eli. Be useful." It was the kind of instruction that sounded simple and turned out to have teeth.

"You rush the catch," Eli tried. "You look up before you've got it."

"You always choke when it counts." Boston said it flatly, quoting somebody, and Eli realized with a small cold feeling that Boston was doing an impression of himself, of a voice he'd heard so often he'd commandeered it as his own. Boston wiped his face with his shirt. "That's what Dylan used to say. Before he moved schools."

"That's not about the catch at all," Eli said.

"It's about me." Boston picked up the ball and spun it once in his hands. "You know the difference between a complaint and criticism? My mom was reading this psychology book, Gottman, it was just lying on the counter, so I picked it up. A complaint is about a specific behavior. Criticism goes after who you are."

Eli looked at him. "You read your mom's psychology book?"

"The good parts." Boston almost smiled. "'You missed practice twice' is a complaint. 'You always mess up' is criticism. Same guy, same situation. One of them you can fix."

The water jugs sat untouched behind them. Across the field the rest of the team had started a scrimmage without Boston, which Eli suspected was half of the problem, the way a group can split people off the way his biology teacher described speciation, one population drifting until they no longer recognize each other as the same team. He didn't say that part out loud.

"Okay," Eli said. "Then here's a complaint. In the drill, you turn your shoulders before the catch. Twice this morning, once Tuesday. That's it. That's the whole list."

Boston stood still for a second, the ball under his arm. "That's a short list," he said.

"Three things. I counted."

"Three things I can fix." He said it slowly, like he was testing the weight of it. Then he set the ball down on the grass, walked back ten yards, and turned. "Throw it. And call out when I turn early, not after."

Eli threw. Boston dropped it, his shoulders rotating a beat before his eyes found the ball.

"That one," Eli said.

They ran it again. This time Boston's head stayed down, stayed down, stayed down, and the ball smacked into his palms and stayed there. He didn't celebrate. He just nodded once, reset his feet, and tapped his chest with both hands. "Again."

On the fifth throw, Emma came over from the scrimmage, hands on her hips, hair stuck to her forehead. "Robinson says you two need to stop hogging the field and get in the rotation."

"In a minute," Boston said, already backing up for another rep. "Tell him I missed the last three scrimmages because of my knee, not because I don't care. Those are different sentences."

Emma looked at Eli, who shrugged. She shrugged back, then jogged off toward midfield.

Boston caught the sixth ball clean and the seventh, and on the eighth he dropped it and laughed, a real laugh, short and surprised out of him. "Specifically," he said, holding up one finger, "that was my left hand."

Eli grinned and backed up another five yards to make it harder. "That's a complaint I can work with."

activity: to check a viral video's source and date with a reverse image search before sharing it
knowledge_domain: to check a viral video's source and date with a reverse image search before sharing it
fact: TinEye, a reverse image search engine launched in 2008, can sort results with the oldest first, helping find when an image first appeared online.
story:
Keaton had his phone flat on the kitchen table before Brayden got his shoes off, screen angled outward like evidence. "Look at this. Look at it." The photo showed a flooded street, a rescue boat nosing past a submerged bus, a woman on a roof holding a dog above the waterline. Below it, a caption in red capitals: BREAKING. LOCAL DAM FAILURE. SHARE BEFORE THEY DELETE THIS.

"They're saying it's forty minutes old," Keaton said. "Some pundit on X already posted it. Two hundred thousand views." His thumb hovered over the share arrow. "I'm putting it in the group chat. Everyone's parents need to see this."

Jayce's mother was at the sink, running water over spinach, and Jayce himself was leaning in the doorway with the particular stillness he saved for Keaton's enthusiasms. "Which dam?" Jayce asked.

"The state's, I don't know, one of them." Keaton flicked through replies, hunting for a location, and found four different towns claimed in four different comments. That should have slowed him. Instead he said, "See, people are confirming it," which was, Brayden thought, like confirming rain by counting umbrellas in a painting.

Brayden pulled out a chair and sat down across from him. He had done this once before, back in the spring, when a photo of a burning courthouse had gone around the sophomore class chat and turned out to be from a movie set. He hadn't caught it himself then; a cousin had, and Brayden had spent the rest of that evening metabolizing the embarrassment, the specific sting of having been confident and wrong in front of people who screenshotted things. "Before you send it," he said, "run the image backwards."

"Run it backwards how?"

"Reverse image search. You put the picture in, it finds where the picture's been." He took Keaton's phone, tipped it toward himself, and opened a browser. "I use TinEye. It's been around since 2008, so its index goes way back." He cropped the photo out of the post, pasted it into the search bar, and hit enter.

The results loaded in a slow, indifferent drip. Keaton drummed the table. Jayce came closer and put both hands on the back of Brayden's chair. At the top of the list there were thumbnails, the same flooded street repeating like a pattern on a roll of fabric, and beside each one a date. Brayden found the sort menu and changed it from newest to oldest. "You can sort them oldest first," he said. "That's how you find when it first showed up online."

The oldest result was dated three years ago. A regional news site, a flood from a typhoon, in a country whose name Brayden had to read twice because it was nowhere near any dam. The woman on the roof had been holding the same dog. The bus had been the same color. Below the photograph the article had a photographer's credit and a caption about monsoon season.

Nobody said anything. The sink shut off. Jayce's mother said, "Dinner's at six, boys," in the voice of someone who had heard nothing, and left the kitchen drying her hands on a towel.

Keaton took his phone back slowly, as if it had changed weight. "It could still be real," he said. "Places flood more than once."

"That's a different picture then," Brayden said. "This one's three years old and an ocean away."

"Some pundit with a million followers posted it. You think he didn't check?"

"I think two hundred thousand people think he checked."

Keaton stared at the typhoon article, scrolling, scrolling, as though somewhere below the credit line there might be an explanation that would give the caption back to him. His share count, Brayden understood, was not a side effect of the post; it was the point of it. Keaton wanted to be first, wanted to be the guy in the group chat who'd known before anyone, and the post had offered him that for the price of one tap. Brayden felt the pull himself, the evanescent glory of having broken news to the room, and he didn't pretend to Jayce afterward that he hadn't. "I would have sent it," he admitted. "Two years ago, without even the search. Probably last month, if I was tired."

"So what do we do?" Jayce asked. "Report it?"

"You can report it. It'll get a hundred thousand more views while you're filling out the form." Brayden was honest about the part he couldn't resolve: the picture was a lie, the caption was a lie, and the flood in it was real, had actually happened, to an actual woman with an actual dog, and somewhere behind that stolen image was a photographer whose work was now a rumor about a dam. Checking the source protected Keaton's group chat. It did nothing for her. He said some of that out loud and Jayce nodded like he was filing it away.

Keaton had gone quiet in a way that was unlike him. Then he laughed, once, short. "Guess who commented asking where it was."

"Who?"

"My uncle. He's a moderator in that group." Keaton turned the phone around. Under the pundit's repost, his uncle's comment sat with a dozen likes: DO NOT SHARE, THIS IS OLD, CHECK YOUR SOURCES. Keaton screenshotted it. "I'm going to post this instead," he said. "Screenshot of the fake, screenshot of the real one, dates side by side."

"Wait," Jayce said. "That's still sharing the fake photo."

"Yeah," Keaton said, thumb already moving, "but now I'm the guy who caught it." He hit post, and the little paper plane flew across the screen.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: The 2026 FIFA World Cup, hosted by Canada, Mexico and the United States, was the first with 48 teams and the first hosted by three countries.
story:
The living room smelled of burnt popcorn and the salsa his mother always made too hot, and Aaron had the remote balanced on his knee like a scepter he hadn't decided how to use. Kellen was sprawled across the armchair claiming it had the best angle for the television, though Aaron suspected he simply liked winning things, even arguments about furniture. Aurelie sat cross-legged on the floor with her phone face down, which for her was a gesture of almost ceremonial respect.

"It's forty-eight teams this year," Kellen said, not looking up from the screen where the pregame analysts were talking over one another. "My cousin keeps saying thirty-two. I told him he's living in the past."

"He is," Aurelie said. "It used to be thirty-two. Now it's forty-eight, and it's the first World Cup three countries have hosted. Canada, Mexico, us."

Aaron, who had been about to say the same thing with more authority, closed his mouth. There was a particular sting in being second to a fact you'd known first, or thought you had.

His father came through with a tray of glasses, ice clinking, impervious to the tension that had nothing to do with him. "Grandpa would have loved this," he said to the room in general, and Aaron nodded because that was the script. Grandpa had watched every tournament since 1986, or that was the story Aaron told, and he had built his whole idea of the man on it: the apartment on Delancey, the small television, the two of them watching a final that had gone to penalties. Aaron could still describe the jersey he'd been wearing. He described it often, sometimes to people who hadn't asked.

The whistle blew and the game assembled itself out of noise. In the fourteenth minute a midfielder took a touch Aaron didn't like, and he said so, loudly, and Kellen told him to let the man breathe. That was their old rhythm, argument as affection, and it carried them through the first half while his mother shouted commentary from the kitchen and Ms. Kerr, the neighbor who had invited herself over with a plate of lemon squares and the air of someone doing them a favor, asked sensible questions from the couch. She wanted to know why there were so many teams all of a sudden. "It's the first time with forty-eight," Aurelie told her again, patiently. "First time hosted by three countries, too." Ms. Kerr said that sounded complicated, and Kellen said it sounded like more games, and Aaron said more games meant more chances for a small country to ruin somebody's month, and for a while they were all talking at once and it was good.

At halftime his father went out to the car for the umbrella Elias had left, because rain was coming, though the sky showed nothing. While he was gone, Ms. Kerr asked Aaron whether his grandfather had really been the fan everyone said. "He used to fall asleep in the second half," she said, mild as milk. "Every match. Your father would carry on watching with the sound off."

Aaron laughed, and then didn't. "That's not," he started, and stopped, because the image he had was so clear: Grandpa upright, both of them yelling at the penalties. But he checked the memory the way you check a pocket and found it thinner than it had been. The jersey he always described, the blue one, had been his own. He had been wearing it in that apartment; the Grandpa in the picture wore it because Aaron had dressed him in it afterward, year by year, telling the story better each time until the telling was the memory. He did not know what to do with the actual man, the one who dozed and let a boy keep the volume low.

He wanted to externalize something then, to say it out loud so it would stop rearranging him privately, and he almost did. Aurelie was right there with her face-down phone. Instead he got more popcorn, because some things you owe yourself first, and when he came back his father was in the doorway shaking rain off the umbrella that wasn't needed yet, and Elias was awake now in the high chair, banging a spoon, and the second half was starting.

"Forty-eight teams," Kellen said again during a lull, mostly to hear himself confirm the world. "Three countries. First time for both."

"I know," Aaron said. "I've known." He watched the ball move, and beside him on the couch Ms. Kerr ate her own lemon square, and his father sat down, and the score was still nothing to nothing, and anything could still happen in it.

activity: graduating from high school
knowledge_domain: graduating from high school
fact: The word valedictorian comes from the Latin vale dicere, meaning "to say farewell," which is why the valedictorian gives a farewell speech.
story:
The folding chairs had been set out on the football field in rows so straight they looked ruled, and Claire sat in the third one with the speech folded into quarters inside her gown pocket, worrying the paper's crease until it went soft. The sun sat high and merciless behind the goalposts. She was valedictorian, which had seemed like an abstract honor until three days ago, when Ms. Sandhu handed her a card with "10 minutes, Claire, that's all you get" written on it, and the abstract became a very concrete five hundred words she could not finish.

The problem was the goodbye. Everything else she could do. She could thank the teachers without groveling, she could name the blackout junior year and the canceled season and the flood in the west stairwell, and people would laugh in the right places. But the last paragraph kept curdling into something off a greeting card, every version worse than the last. She'd written "as we scatter like seeds" and deleted it so fast the keys were still warm.

Beside her, Giuliano kept checking his phone inside his sleeve like a spy with somewhere better to be, which, it turned out, he had. "The 2:40 bus," he said under the processional music. "Job interview in the city. If I abscond right after they hand us the folders, I make it. If I wait for the whole receiving line, I don't." He said it lightly, the way he said everything, but she could see the arithmetic going on behind his eyes, cost of the taxi versus cost of being late, and she understood that for him this ceremony was a fence to get over, not a moment to keep.

"You're not skipping my speech," Melinda said from his other side, leaning across him with her camera already out. She wanted the photo, the one with all three of them and the scoreboard behind them reading CONGRATULATES SENIORS, wanted it before the light went flat and before anyone's family claimed them. She'd been talking about it for a week, planning it like a military operation. "After the folders, before the line. Two minutes."

"Two minutes," Giuliano agreed, which was a negotiation, not a promise, and Claire noted that everyone she loved was trying to take a different thing out of this field, and none of those things were hers to give.

While the principal read the names of the school board, she took out the speech one more time and looked at the first line of the cursed paragraph, "And now, as we part," and thought, not for the first time, that Latin had ruined her. Four years of it. Somewhere in her binder at home was a page of roots from September, and something about the word valedictorian had been on it, she was almost sure, a fact that had seemed like trivia then and now felt like a door. She thumbed through her photos until she found the one she'd taken of that page, the flash bleaching the ink, and there it was in her own handwriting: vale dicere, to say farewell. She turned to Melinda and showed her the screen. "It means to say farewell," she said. "That's the whole word. That's why the valedictorian gives a farewell speech." The valedictorian, she thought, is not the best student. The valedictorian is the one who says goodbye. They had given her the job of leaving, formally, on behalf of everyone, and she had been trying to decorate it with seeds and scattering when all the word asked her to do was say the thing plainly.

She turned the program over and wrote on the back of it in the margin by the dentist advertisement: the speech is not about how great we were. It's about the fact that this is over, and that we're the ones who have to say so. Her erudition, such as it was, had finally produced something usable, one small fact doing the work of a whole paragraph. She didn't know yet if the audience would hear it that way, whether three hundred families in folding chairs wanted the truth or the greeting card, and she decided, folding the program back into her pocket, that she was about to find out in the most public way possible.

When Ms. Sandhu's turn on the podium came and went, brief and dry as promised, the principal began reading names, and the line of gowns shuffled forward like an incipient avalanche, slow, then less slow. Giuliano collected his folder with a fist pump aimed at the sky and drifted toward the fence with his duffel already over his shoulder. Melinda grabbed Claire's arm. "Now, before they release the rows," she said, hauling her toward the scoreboard, camera up, sun behind them for once.

Claire stood where she was put, smiled for the picture, and heard the principal's voice over the loudspeaker saying they would reconvene for the valedictory address in five minutes. On the back of her program, in the margin, the new first line of the last paragraph was drying. She could see Giuliano at the gate, one foot already through it, and she raised her hand and called his name across the grass.

"Claire," Melinda said, "hold still."

"I'll be one second." She cupped her hands around her mouth. "Vale," she called, and Giuliano turned, and after a beat he called it back.

activity: applying to college and waiting for the answer
knowledge_domain: applying to college and waiting for the answer
fact: Early Decision in US college admissions is binding: a student admitted with acceptable financial aid must enroll and withdraw all other applications.
story:
The printer on the second floor of the public library took forty seconds per page, and Juliette had timed it, because she had printed her Early Decision agreement three times already without signing it. She sat at the table by the window with the form in front of her, a pen from her backpack, and her phone face down beside the copy machine receipt. The deadline was eleven days away. Pellston University wanted the form by the first of November, signed by her and by a parent, and her mother had already signed, on the kitchen counter, without reading past the first line.

Paxton dropped into the chair across from her with a stack of SAT prep books he had no intention of opening. "You're still on that?"

"It's binding," Juliette said. "That's the whole thing. If they take me and the financial aid is enough, I have to go. And I have to pull all my other applications."

"Enough by whose math?"

"Mine, I guess. Theirs." She turned the form over. On the back, in smaller print, the same sentence appeared again, that admitted students must enroll and withdraw applications elsewhere. It said acceptable financial aid. It did not say what happened if the aid was unacceptable, and she had read the paragraph four times looking for that part.

Braxton arrived ten minutes late, as always, carrying two coffees and half a muffin. He put one coffee in front of Juliette, which she took as a peace offering for something he had not yet admitted to. "Ms. Tran said you were up here," he said. "She's downstairs doing the tax forms for old people again."

"Did she say anything else?"

"She said you looked like someone deciding whether to jump off something."

Paxton laughed. Juliette didn't. She slid the form across to Braxton, who read faster than either of them and had a way of getting to the part that mattered. "So you apply, you get in, they give you a package," he said. "And if the package works, you're done. You enroll, you cancel everything else."

"Every other application. Yes."

"And if the package doesn't work?"

"That's what I can't find out ahead of time. I don't know what they'll offer until they offer it. And I don't know what the other schools would have offered, because I won't have applied, or I'll have had to withdraw them." She heard her own voice go flat on the last part, the way it did when she was close to the thing she actually wanted to say. "Riverton gave Paxton's sister a full ride two years ago. Same numbers as me, roughly. But Riverton doesn't do this. I could apply there regular and find out in March."

Paxton leaned back until the chair creaked. "So apply regular everywhere. What's the problem?"

"The acceptance rate is higher this way. That's what everybody says. You commit, they like it." She had a brochure in her bag that used the word demonstrate, as in demonstrated interest, and she had read it so many times the phrase had worn smooth. "If I go regular, I'm in a pile with everyone else. If I go early, I'm in a smaller pile of people who promised."

Braxton tore his muffin in half and gave her the larger half, which she took as a second offering. "So it's a trade," he said. "Better odds now, or better information later."

"That's it. That's exactly it." She said it without effusive relief, because relief wasn't quite the word either; it was more like the feeling of someone taking a heavy bag from her arms, and her arms not knowing what to do.

Ms. Tran came up at four to collect stray books from the tables. She had been the young adult librarian since before any of them could drive, and she had a policy of never telling students what to do, which Juliette had tested more than once. Ms. Tran picked up the form, glanced at it, and set it back down with the pen squared against its edge.

"You know," Ms. Tran said, "the reference desk has the financial aid handbook, the one with all the school profiles in it. Average aid, by school. Not what they'll give you. What they've given."

"An average," Juliette said.

"An average is a place to stand." Ms. Tran gathered the prep books Paxton had never opened and carried them off toward the shelving cart.

Juliette sat for a while with her hands in her lap. She was thinking of two things at once, which she had learned to do slowly rather than all at once: the smaller pile and the sealed envelope of the average, the promise and the comparison she would never get to make. She could not hold both as true in the same moment, and she was beginning to suspect that choosing was not the same as resolving.

She got up, went down one floor, and found the handbook on the shelf where Ms. Tran had said. She carried it to the copy machine, and her heart palpitated once, hard, when she put in her quarters. Paxton's voice came down the stairwell after her, calling her name, and she fed the first page into the glass.

activity: taking a first driving lesson
knowledge_domain: taking a first driving lesson
fact: Under the two-second rule, a driver watches the car ahead pass a fixed point, such as a sign, and checks that at least two seconds pass before reaching that same point.
story:
The parking lot behind the closed hardware store had been empty since March, and Savannah sat in the driver's seat of Ms. Grewal's hatchback with her hands at ten and two, waiting to be told she was doing it wrong. Ms. Grewal had a clipboard she never wrote on and a voice like she was narrating a nature documentary, calm to the point of parody.

"Reverse out of the space, nice and slow," Ms. Grewal said. "Feet are for the pedals, hands are for the wheel. Nothing else exists."

Savannah had wanted this lesson for months, had saved for it out of her shifts at the pharmacy, because in September she would be forty minutes from campus and her mother would not be driving her. The want was simple and enormous: to be the kind of person who could leave when she chose to. The problem was that the car seemed to have opinions of its own. She reversed, checked her mirror too late, and clipped a shopping cart with the rear bumper, a sound like a bell being murdered. The cart rolled lazily across three empty spaces and came to rest against a faded sign for the two-dollar bin.

"I hit a cart," Savannah said. "In an empty lot."

"It happens," said Ms. Grewal. "Now drive us out to the road. Turn left."

The road was busier than she had expected for a Tuesday evening, a slow procession of cars coming home from somewhere. Savannah merged, or rather appeared, and within two minutes she had drifted up behind a blue sedan so close that she could count the crumbs on the driver's shoulder through the rear window. She hadn't noticed herself doing it. It was like the way she used to sit closer and closer to the television, some gravity in the thing ahead pulling her forward.

"Give yourself some room," Ms. Grewal said, mildly, the way you'd mention weather.

Savannah eased off, and then, within thirty seconds, crept back up. Twice more. Her father, when she'd asked him about driving, had delivered a trenchant little speech about how people who tailgated were idiots who deserved what they got, and she had nodded along at the kitchen table, feeling superior to a category of person she was apparently becoming. That was the trouble with his speeches. They sorted the world into the guilty and the smart, and never told you how the smart stayed smart.

"There's a lamppost coming up on the right," Ms. Grewal said. "Watch the car ahead pass it. Then count until you reach that same point."

"One Mississippi, two Mississippi," Savannah said under her breath as the sedan cleared the lamppost, and then again as she passed it herself. Two seconds, barely. Three feet of asphalt, maybe less, between her bumper and his.

"You know it's called the two-second rule," Ms. Grewal said. "At least two seconds behind the car ahead, from any fixed point to that same point. Under two, you're too close."

Savannah dropped back until she counted a full two Mississippis, and the strangest thing happened in her chest. The road opened. The sedan stopped being a wall and became an object at a distance, something she could watch rather than something she was falling toward. She could see past it, see the brake lights two cars ahead, see the intersection and the light turning amber early enough to decide, not just react. Room to think turned out to be an actual, physical thing you could give yourself, measured in Mississippis against a lamppost.

Her mother would have called this a lesson and made it a metaphor by dessert. Her father would have litigated it, demanded evidence that two seconds beat three, subpoenaed the driving manual, cross-examined Ms. Grewal until the whole business was a courtroom and Savannah a hostile witness. They were both like that, which was maybe why the house had gotten so quiet. She didn't want to be either one. She wanted the version where you notice you're too close to something, and you let off the gas, and you count, and no one has to win.

At the next red light she stopped with the sedan's bumper well ahead of her, counted her two seconds against a stop sign on the corner, and said, out loud, mostly to herself, "I'm going to do that every time. Until it's automatic. Then I'll stop having to count, I guess, and I won't even know I'm doing it." She heard how it sounded, a promise made in the absence of proof, and she let it stand anyway.

When they pulled back into the empty lot, the shopping cart was still leaning against the two-dollar bin sign, and Ms. Grewal said nothing about it, which Savannah understood as a form of grace. She parked between the faded white lines on the first try, straighter than she'd expected, and turned the key. The engine died with a small shudder, like the car agreeing to stop pretending.

"Same time next week," Ms. Grewal said, making her first mark on the clipboard.

Savannah got out and stood a moment in the flat evening light, looking at the cart, then walked over and pushed it back toward the store, its bad wheel shrieking all the way across the lot.

activity: taking a first driving lesson
knowledge_domain: taking a first driving lesson
fact: According to the CDC, US drivers aged 16 to 19 have a fatal crash rate almost three times as high as drivers aged 20 and older, per mile driven.
story:
Logan sat in the driver's seat of Ms. Ramos's old sedan with his hands at ten and two, exactly where the pamphlet said, and stared at the faded lines of the parking lot outside the closed supermarket. Ms. Ramos lived three doors down and had offered to teach him before his mother got around to it, which his mother described as a kindness and Logan privately suspected was also a way for Ms. Ramos to feel useful on Sunday mornings. He turned the key. The engine caught on the second try, and the whole car seemed to shudder awake around him, a machine much larger than he had imagined from the passenger seat.

"Foot on the brake before you put it in gear," Ms. Ramos said. "Always the brake first." She said it without alarm, the way people repeat rules they have repeated for decades. Logan pressed the pedal, moved the shift into drive, and felt the car strain forward against his foot like a dog on a leash.

He had gotten his permit two weeks ago. He'd stood in the licensing office for over an hour next to Celia, who was there for the same reason, and while they waited she had read the safety posters aloud to entertain herself. One of them she read twice. According to the CDC, it said, drivers aged sixteen to nineteen had a fatal crash rate almost three times as high as drivers aged twenty and older, per mile driven. "Almost three times," Celia had repeated, looking at him. "That's us, Logan. That's the category we just joined." She'd said it lightly, the way she said most things, and then she'd passed her test and gone home.

He had thought about it since, more than he wanted to admit. Not the statistic itself, which felt abstract, but the strange idea that a number could describe him before he'd done anything. He hadn't driven into a ditch or texted behind a wheel; he hadn't even merged onto a highway. And yet the poster had already sorted him into a group, the way the school sorted students by GPA, and he resented it and half believed it at the same time.

"Ease off the brake," Ms. Ramos said. "Let it roll. Don't touch the gas yet." He let his foot up a fraction and the car glided forward, smoother than he expected, almost beguiling in how little effort it took, as if the lot were tilted in his favor. He turned the wheel a little and the car followed, obedient, and for one bright second he thought, this is easy, I don't know what everyone is so afraid of. Then he remembered that everyone being afraid was the point of the poster, and the second dimmed.

He practiced stopping at the faded cart-return corral as if it were a stop sign, then practiced turning around the light poles. Ms. Ramos was parsimonious with praise, offering "good" maybe three times in twenty minutes, which somehow made each one worth more than a paragraph of encouragement from his mother would have been. Abdul had texted him a photo of a scraped mailbox that morning with the caption "day one energy," and Logan had laughed and then, unexpectedly, hadn't.

"You're gripping too hard," Ms. Ramos said. "Loosen your thumbs. You don't steer with your knuckles, you steer with your palms." He loosened. In the back of his mind he was still working on the poster, on the two ways of hearing it. His mother's way was that it proved sixteen was too young, that he should wait a year, maybe two, until the danger passed out of him the way a fever breaks. Celia's way was that it proved nothing about her, that statistics described populations and she was a person. He could see the appeal of both. What he couldn't see was a way to hold them at once without pretending one of them away, and he was tired of pretending.

"Can I ask you something?" he said. "Do you think sixteen is too young to drive?" Ms. Ramos was quiet for a moment, watching the far end of the lot where a single shopping cart stood askew against a curb. "I think I've known careful seventeen-year-olds and reckless fifty-year-olds," she said, "and I've known the opposite. Now turn here and come back along the front of the store." Logan turned the wheel, palms this time not knuckles, and the car swung in a wide, imperfect arc that straightened as he corrected it. The cart by the curb caught the low morning light, and he drove toward it, slow, both hands loose on the wheel.

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: Mixing paints is subtractive: each pigment absorbs some wavelengths of light, so mixing many pigments together tends toward a dark, muddy color rather than white.
story:
The paint on Samuel's palette knife had gone the color of a riverbank, and he had started with yellow. He was trying to repaint the sign that hung over his grandmother's garden gate, a wooden board with her name and a border of marigolds, and the marigolds had become his nemesis. Every orange he mixed came out duller than the one before, as though the pigments were conspiring against brightness rather than building toward it.

He had dragged a folding table into the backyard that morning and laid out the tubes his mother had bought at the craft store, the cheap ones with the screw caps that never quite closed. The yard was long and narrow, fenced in cedar, with a vegetable patch at the far end where the tomatoes had begun to lean on their stakes. He worked with the board propped against an upturned milk crate, and he had been at it for two hours.

Jax arrived around noon, cutting through the gap in the back fence as he had been doing since they were nine. He stood behind Samuel for a while, eating an apple, watching the knife turn the yellow-red mixture in slow circles.

"It keeps going brown," Samuel said. "I keep thinking if I add more of the bright one, more yellow, it'll come back. It doesn't come back."

Jax leaned over the table. "Add white."

Samuel added white. The mixture went pale and chalky, a peach that had given up, and neither of them said anything for a moment.

Later Skyla came by with her sketchbook under her arm, and when she looked at the palette she made a small sound, not quite a laugh. "That's subtractive," she said. "Paint, I mean. Each pigment absorbs some wavelengths of light, so the more you mix in, the more gets absorbed. You pile enough pigments together and you don't get white, you get that." She pointed at the muddy pile on the knife. "It's not you. It's physics."

Samuel looked at the board, at the clean orange of the remaining marigolds he had not touched, then at the sludge on his palette. "So the whole morning was a lesson in subtraction."

"Basically."

He scraped the knife clean against the edge of the table and thought about it while Skyla flipped open her sketchbook and Jax pitched his apple core into the compost. His instinct, the one he had followed all morning, was that adding was the way to get more of something. More pigment, more color, more brightness. But the paint kept only what it refused to absorb, and every new pigment took something away. He was not sure the idea stopped at paint. He thought of arguments he had watched curdle in group chats, everyone adding their layer until the whole thing was unrecognizable, and he was not sure whether that was the same principle or just a convenient metaphor, and he decided he did not have to decide yet.

He tried again with the dirty orange, this time from the other direction. He squeezed a fresh pile of yellow and touched in the smallest bead of red he could manage, barely enough to tint it, and the marigold color appeared at once, warm and bright, closer to the flower itself than anything he had made all day. He painted one full bloom before he let himself sit back. It had not required more. It had required restraint, which was a way of thinking he had not been inured to, raised as he was on the assumption that problems yielded to effort applied in quantity.

Ms. Mansour, the neighbor whose yard backed onto theirs, called over the fence that the flower was the best thing on the board. She said her own mother had grown marigolds, that in her family's village they were practically autochthonous, springing up wherever the ground was left alone for a season. Samuel thanked her and looked at the untouched corner of the board, where the original paint, faded by eight summers of weather, still held a pale ghost of the orange he had been chasing.

He cleaned his brushes in the jar of water, which had turned the same muddy brown as his failures, and set the board in the shade to dry. There were four more marigolds to paint, and he knew now that he would paint them with almost nothing on the knife, the smallest portion of red the yellow would carry. Jax asked if he could try one, and Samuel handed him a fresh brush, tube of red still uncapped in his hand, watching how much his friend took.

activity: getting a first part-time job
knowledge_domain: getting a first part-time job
fact: Under the US Fair Labor Standards Act, non-exempt employees must be paid one and a half times their regular rate for hours worked beyond 40 in a workweek.
story:
Henry got the job the week school let out, which felt like a small miracle until his first paycheck arrived and he understood how little eleven dollars an hour actually was. He sat at the kitchen table with the stub flattened under the desk lamp, doing the arithmetic twice, because the numbers did not match what he'd expected. Some of his hours had been paid at a higher rate, sixteen fifty, and at first he assumed the payroll office had made an error in his favor, the kind of error you keep quiet about.

He brought it up anyway, the next morning, standing at the edge of the guard station while Oscar folded towels.

"Check your stub," Henry said. "Did some of yours come out at a different rate?"

Oscar squinted at the chlorine-glare off the water. "Mine's all the same. I only worked thirty hours."

"I picked up Marisol's shifts, though. I had forty-eight." Henry had volunteered for every extra shift anyone offered, partly for the money and partly because the pool in the early morning, before the camps arrived, had a hush he liked, a kind of asceticism, the whistle silent, the water unmoving, nothing to do but watch.

Douglas ambled over from the front desk with a clipboard. "It's overtime," he said. "My cousin gets it at the grocery store. Under the law, once you go past forty hours in a week, they have to pay you one and a half times your regular rate for the extra hours. Forty-eight means eight hours at sixteen fifty for you."

"Nobody told me that."

"Nobody told me either. I asked when my cousin's check looked weird." Douglas shrugged. "I figured you knew. You read things."

Henry turned this over.
