He had not known, and the discovery sat strangely with him, half pleasure at the money and half embarrassment that he had nearly vilified the payroll office for a generosity that turned out to be the law. He'd been ready to feel like a thief. Instead he'd been a beneficiary of a rule he'd never bothered to learn.

That afternoon Mr. Jean-Louis, the facility manager, called him into the office about the schedule for the Fourth of July week. The camps were doubling their pool time and he needed guards.

"You're my reliable one," Mr. Jean-Louis said. "I can put you at fifty, fifty-five hours if you want it. The overtime will cost the district, but we're short-staffed, so it's that or close the shallow end." He said it without drama, a man laying out facts.

Henry said yes before he'd thought it through, and then thought about it for two days. He thought about his father, who had worked nights at the plant for years and once said, in the car, that the money had been good and the years had gone somewhere he couldn't find them again. Henry had always taken that as a warning against greed. But sitting in the tall chair on Saturday, watching a line of incipient thunderheads build in the west over the diving well, he decided he'd taken it wrong, or at least incompletely. His father hadn't been warning him off work. He'd been describing a trade he would make again, Henry suspected, if the kids were young and the rent was due. The warning and the endorsement were the same sentence, and which one you heard depended on what you needed.

On Monday he found Mr. Jean-Louis before the camps arrived.

"I'll do the fifty hours," Henry said. "But not fifty-five. Douglas wants some of the holiday shifts, if you can split them."

Mr. Jean-Louis looked at him over the schedule grid. "More money is more money."

"I know." Henry had changed his mind about that, or at least about how much of it he wanted to want. The extra pay was real, and he would use it, and he was not going to pretend the math didn't matter. But he'd also realized, sometime between the whistle drills and the afternoon glare, that he liked having a morning where nobody expected him anywhere, and that no rate, regular or multiplied, could buy one back after it was spent.

"Just so you know," Douglas said later, toweling off by the drain grate, "you're giving up like eighty bucks."

"More than that. It's one and a half times for the extra ones."

"Still."

"I know," Henry said again. He wasn't sure he'd made the right choice, and he noticed that the uncertainty didn't bother him the way it would have a month ago, when every decision had felt like a door that locked behind you. He climbed back into the chair, adjusted the umbrella against the climbing sun, and watched the first school bus pull into the lot, its doors folding open with a hiss he could hear all the way across the deck.

activity: to predict how a change in temperature shifts a reaction at equilibrium using Le Chatelier's principle
knowledge_domain: to predict how a change in temperature shifts a reaction at equilibrium using Le Chatelier's principle
fact: If the forward reaction is endothermic, raising the temperature shifts the equilibrium toward the products.
story:
The kettle had just clicked off when Logan spread his chemistry notes across the kitchen table, flattening the curled corner of the page with the sugar bowl. Tomorrow was the retake, and Ms. Tanaka had written one line on his last attempt: "You know the words. You don't yet know which way things move." He had stared at it for two days without understanding what she meant, and now the exam was fourteen hours away.

Samir arrived first, shaking rain off his jacket, followed by Jessica, who claimed the chair nearest the window so she could see the street. She wanted to leave early for her brother's birthday dinner, and she said so immediately, as though declaring a deadline to the room might make the universe propitiate her with a fast hour of studying. Samir, by contrast, seemed prepared to stay until the kettle gave out. He set down his own notes with the gravity of a man who intended to win something.

"Question four," he said, tapping Logan's sheet. "The reaction takes in heat going forward. If you warm it up, which way does it go?"

"Products," Logan said, because that was what his notes said, and then, because he heard himself sounding like a recording, he stopped.

"Toward the reactants," Jessica said at the same moment. "Heat is a product of the forward direction, sort of. Adding heat pushes it backward." She had a way of saying things with complete certainty that made Logan doubt himself even when he had written the opposite in ink. Samir shook his head, and the argument began in earnest, low and steady, the way their arguments always went, like weather that refused to become a storm.

Logan got up and poured the tea, thinking that this was exactly the hole Ms. Tanaka had pointed at. He could recite the rule, but when two people he trusted disagreed in his own kitchen, he had nothing to stand on. He carried three mugs back, set them down, and said, "Neither of you move. I'm going to find out, and not from my notes." He opened his laptop and pulled up the equilibrium simulation Ms. Tanaka had linked in the class portal months ago, the one he had skipped and privately considered beneath him, the habit of a misanthrope who would rather be confused alone than seen using training wheels.

On the screen he set up a reaction that absorbed heat going forward, with the forward direction marked endothermic, and let it settle. The bar graphs on each side steadied, blue on the left, amber on the right, balanced but not equal. "Watch," he said. He slid the temperature control upward.

The bars moved. The amber side, the products, grew as the blue side shrank, slowly at first and then with something almost seismic in the little interface, the whole system lurching toward the right and then settling again into a new stillness. Jessica leaned in, and her certainty, which usually survived anything, visibly rearranged itself. "Okay," she said. "Okay. If the forward reaction is endothermic, raising the temperature shifts the equilibrium toward the products. I had it backwards." She said it plainly, without drama, and Samir sat back with the small satisfied stillness of a person who had been right but cared more about the demonstration than the victory.

"Run it cold," Samir said, so Logan did, dragging the temperature down, and they watched the blue side reclaim what it had lost. He ran it three more times, faster, slower, with different starting amounts, and each time the direction held. That was the part he had never understood, he realized: the rule wasn't a sentence to memorize but a direction things actually moved, and he had watched it move. What he still couldn't have said was why the molecules obeyed it, only that they did, and that Ms. Tanaka's exam would not ask him why.

Jessica packed up at six, blowing on her hands although the kitchen was warm, and promised to text if the dinner cake turned out as badly as she feared. Samir stayed another twenty minutes, quizzing Logan with the flashcards neither of them had needed since the simulation, and then left his lucky pen on the table on purpose, telling Logan to keep it until after the exam and return it afterward, which was Samir's way of arranging a future in which there would be an afterward. Logan sat alone with the two cold teas and the one still steaming, opened his notes, and read the sentence about endothermic reactions again. This time it sounded less like a sentence and more like something he had seen happen. He picked up the lucky pen, turned to a blank page, and wrote at the top: "Heat is a direction. Tomorrow, point it."

activity: applying to college and waiting for the answer
knowledge_domain: applying to college and waiting for the answer
fact: The SAT switched to a digital, adaptive format in the United States in March 2024: how well a student does on the first module of each section sets the difficulty of the second.
story:
The results portal opened at five, and at 4:52 Abigail was still in Mr. Tan's classroom, turning a piece of chalk over in her fingers instead of writing the warm-up problem on the board.

"You're not going to solve it by staring," Mr. Tan said. He was erasing the previous period's work, and the dust settled on his sleeves like sedimentary layers, the old classes compacted under the new. "And you're not going to solve your score either."

"I'm not staring at the score. I'm staring at the chalk." She set it down anyway.

Maliyah came in with a bag of chips and no intention of doing the warm-up. She sat on the desk beside Abigail's, which was against the rules, and tore the bag open, which was also against the rules, and offered it to Mr. Tan, who took three chips without looking up from his erasing. This was the entire basis of their relationship.

"It went badly," Abigail said. "The second math module. It was brutal. Like, questions I'd never seen before, weird ones. Which means I bombed the first one and they gave up on me."

"That's not what it means." Maliyah licked salt off her thumb. "You took it in April, right? After they switched. It's adaptive now. How you do on the first module of each section sets the difficulty of the second. Hard second module means you did well on the first. You got the easy questions, so it gave you the hard ones."

Abigail looked at her. "That's a real thing?"

"That's a real thing. Mary figured it out because her brother panicked about the same thing last month and their mom called the school counselor at nine at night. Adaptive. One word, whole system." Maliyah shrugged. "So the module you're calling brutal is probably the reward module."

"It didn't feel like a reward."

"Rewards rarely do."

The clock said 4:56. Abigail had spent the four days since the test constructing and then demolishing the same argument, and it bothered her that Maliyah's version was more persuasive and had taken eleven seconds. She had assumed the test was like a steppe, flat and endless, the same ground for everyone, and her ground had clearly been rockier, therefore she was worse. But if the ground under her had been rockier because someone had looked at her first mile and decided she could handle rock, then the whole comparison collapsed. Not just the score. The way she'd been reading everyone else's complaints, too. Mary had said the math was easy, and Abigail had let that impugn her own preparation for days, and Mary had apparently started with a first module so bad that her second module was practically arithmetic with friendly fonts.

"I've been ranking myself against people who took a different test," Abigail said.

"Congratulations. That's the most expensive realization of your senior year."

Mr. Tan put the eraser down. "Eight minutes," he said. "And I'll note that neither of you has done the warm-up, which is why the chips are staying out on the desk where I can see them."

Abigail got out her phone. The login page asked for her date of birth, which felt like a bureaucratic joke, as though a stranger might try to steal her SAT score. She typed it. The little wheel spun. She thought, with a clarity she did not trust, that both of her theories were still possible. The hard module could mean she'd earned it, or Maliyah could have the mechanism wrong, or the adaptation could be coarse and imperfect, a machine sorting thousands of people into two bins and calling that precision. She could hold both versions. She could look at the number and still not know which one had been true, only what the number was.

"Stop narrating your face," Maliyah said. "Open it."

She opened it. The page loaded in stages, which she would remember later as an act of institutional cruelty: first the header, then the date, then the score, arriving like a bus.

She read it twice. Then she turned the phone face down on the desk, took a chip, and said, "Mary owes me an apology and also a coffee."

"That good?"

"That weird," Abigail said. "It's better than my practice tests and worse than what I wanted, and I have no idea which module did it, and I'm going to be fine with that by tomorrow. Possibly Thursday."

Mr. Tan collected the chip bag, wrote the warm-up problem on the board in his patient, layered chalk, and tapped the board twice. "Solve it," he said. "It's a hard one."

activity: applying to college and waiting for the answer
knowledge_domain: applying to college and waiting for the answer
fact: Need-blind admission means a college decides whom to admit without considering whether the applicant can afford to pay; many US colleges are instead need-aware.
story:
The portal had been open in a browser tab for eleven days, which was nine days longer than Isabelle had planned. The little orange dot that meant "application received" had not changed color, and she had begun to treat it like a pet, checking it before school, after school, once at two in the morning when she couldn't sleep. Her mother kept saying not to jinx it by watching, and then standing behind the desk chair with a dish towel in her hands, watching too.

The real work, though, was the spreadsheet. Isabelle had twelve colleges listed in it, twelve tabs' worth of tuition numbers, and the numbers did what numbers do, which is refuse to shrink. Her family could pay something, but the something was small, and she had spent the weekend doing what she called research and her mother called worrying with the lid open. On a Sunday afternoon she opened a video call with Selina, who was lying on her bed upside down, and said, "Okay, I need you to look at something and tell me if I'm crazy."

"You're crazy," Selina said, but she sat up.

Isabelle shared her screen. "So I thought all these places just looked at your grades and your essay and decided. That's what I assumed. But they don't all do it the same way." She scrolled to the column she'd added that morning, the one with two letters repeated down it. "Some of them are need-blind. That means they decide who to admit without even looking at whether you can afford to pay. They don't know. It never comes into it."

"That's good, right?"

"For those, yes. But look at the rest of my list." Seven of the twelve had the other letters, and Isabelle pointed at them one by one. "Most US colleges aren't like that. A lot of them are need-aware, which is the opposite. They can see what your family can pay, and it's part of the decision." She heard her own voice get flat on the last word, the way it did when she was trying to sound like a scientist instead of a person.

Selina was quiet for a second, which was unusual for Selina. "So when you applied to those seven, they knew."

"They knew."

Downstairs, the doorbell rang, and then Mr. Mendoza's voice came up the stairwell, asking whether anyone had ordered the package that had been left at his house by mistake. Isabelle carried the box up to her room and found him already at the top of the stairs, and somehow the spreadsheet came up, because everything came up with Mr. Mendoza, who had once been a high school counselor and knew how to ask the second question after the first one. He looked at her screen for a while without touching anything.

"You've been honest in your applications?" he asked.

"Brutally honest. I wrote the essay about Mom's hours getting cut. I said I was a polymath in the activities section, which Heidi told me sounded arrogant, but it's true, I do everything half-well and two things well." She laughed, and heard that it wasn't really a laugh. "Maybe I shouldn't have. Maybe it looks scattered."

"It looks like a person," Mr. Mendoza said. "The finances you can't change by worrying about them on a Sunday." He set the box on her desk, thanked her mother, and left, and Isabelle felt both better and worse, which she was starting to understand was the ordinary condition of waiting.

That night she and Heidi sat in the same call on mute, doing homework in parallel, the way they did before exams. Isabelle kept the spreadsheet open behind her physics problems. She had been telling herself for two weeks that the schools at the top of her list were reaches because they were prestigious, and tonight, finally, she let herself read the sentence she'd written in her own notes: they're reaches partly because of money, and I knew that when I clicked submit. It had been easier to believe she was only up against her transcript. She moved three of the need-aware schools down and moved two need-blind ones up, not because they were kinder, because she couldn't know that, but because she had decided she wanted at least half her list to be places where the orange dot was judging one thing only.

"I'm rearranging my whole future at eleven p.m.," she said out loud, unmuting.

Heidi looked up from her lab report. "Should you be doing that now?"

"Probably not. Probably I should sleep." Isabelle saved the file, closed the laptop halfway so the light dimmed but the machine stayed on, and left the spreadsheet glowing faintly through the gap like something still breathing.

The next morning, before school, she checked the portal first, the way she always did. The orange dot had turned green.

activity: how interest makes borrowed money cost more over time and makes savings grow
knowledge_domain: how interest makes borrowed money cost more over time and makes savings grow
fact: Compound interest follows A = P(1 + r/n)^(nt), where n is how many times per year interest is added, so more frequent compounding gives a slightly larger total.
story:
The sign in the window said thirty-six months, zero money down, and Vanessa read it twice before going in, because things that sounded free rarely were. The phone store smelled of warm plastic and lemon cleaner, and a wall of lit screens curved toward her like a display of small moons. She had one hundred and eighty dollars in her sock drawer at home and a mother whose phone had shattered on Tuesday, though nobody in this store knew that yet, and she intended to keep it that way until she understood the numbers.

A man in a gray shirt drifted over and introduced himself as Mr. Baptiste, then laid a glossy sheet on the counter between them. The sheet showed a phone like the one in the window, with a monthly payment printed beneath it, and the payment was small enough to have verisimilitude, which was exactly what made her wary. She had learned in English class that the most convincing details were the ones you were meant not to question.

"Twenty-four dollars a month," Mr. Baptiste said. "For thirty-six months."

She did the arithmetic in her head, slow and unglamorous. Twenty-four times thirty-six was eight hundred sixty-four. The phone's cash price, printed in a smaller font on the same sheet, was six hundred ninety-nine. So the difference, a hundred and sixty-five dollars, was what borrowing cost, quiet as dust settling. "So I'd pay extra for paying over time," she said, and he smiled and said that was how financing worked, that nothing was free, and she appreciated that he didn't pretend otherwise.

Behind her, Sienna was examining a case shaped like a cassette tape, and Bastien had drifted to a kiosk near the register where the credit union kept a stack of brochures, because apparently the credit union had a partnership with the store, a small table with a pen chained to it. He held up a brochure. "Vanessa. Come look at this. Two savings accounts. Same rate. Different totals."

She took it from him. The page showed two examples side by side, both starting with the same principal, both at the same rate, but one account compounded monthly and the other yearly, and the monthly one ended slightly larger. At the bottom, in a thin serif font, sat the formula, A = P(1 + r/n)^(nt), with a note that n was how many times per year interest was added.

"So more frequent compounding gives you a slightly bigger total," Bastien said, tapping the two final numbers.

"It's the mirror of the phone," Vanessa said slowly, and felt something click into place, the way two puzzle pieces refuse and then don't. "Borrowing over time costs more. Saving over time earns more. Same mechanism, opposite direction." She thought of her sock drawer money, desiccating there, doing nothing, shrinking in real terms while prices crept up, and she thought of the hundred and sixty-five dollars the financing would quietly take from her mother, who had three job interviews scheduled and no working phone to receive the calls on.

The withheld thing pushed its way to the front of her mind and she let it out. "It's not for me," she said. "My mom's phone broke. She has interviews starting Monday. I came in to see if there was a cheap refurb, but if I put my hundred and eighty down and finance the rest, the interest makes it worse, and if she gets the job she could pay cash in two weeks anyway."

Mr. Baptiste considered her, then reached under the counter and produced a refurbished model, last year's, with a hairline scratch across the back like a scratch on a montane lake seen from a summit trail. "One forty-nine," he said. "Cash."

She counted out the bills she had brought folded in her back pocket, all of it, leaving nothing in reserve. There was a chance her mother wouldn't get any of the jobs, a chance the phone would be the last thing they bought easily for a while, a chance the hundred and eighty would have been safer in the drawer earning its small compounding fraction. She couldn't know. Sienna snapped her cassette case onto the refurb without being asked, and Bastien slid the brochure across the counter toward Mr. Baptiste as if handing over evidence.

"Keep it," Mr. Baptiste said, pushing it back. "Teach the next one."

Vanessa folded the brochure into eighths and put it in her pocket, next to the receipt and the dead phone she was carrying home in its place.

activity: to write a database query that joins two tables to find which customers ordered nothing
knowledge_domain: to write a database query that joins two tables to find which customers ordered nothing
fact: A LEFT JOIN in SQL returns every row from the left table, filling the right table's columns with NULL wherever no matching row exists.
story:
Evan's grandfather kept two notebooks in the kitchen drawer beside the stove, and both of them were older than Evan. One held the names and phone numbers of every customer who had ever bought a stone from the shop, back when there was a shop; the other held the orders, dated and priced, in a cramped forward-slanting hand. When Evan mentioned offhandedly that he was learning databases, his grandfather set the notebooks on the table and said, "Then tell me who never bought anything."

The problem sounded easy until Evan typed the names into his laptop that evening, one table called Customers and one called Orders, with a column of customer IDs linking them. He wrote a query joining the two tables and ran it. The result came back a tidy list of forty-one rows, every one of them a person who had ordered something. Ray Aldous, three orders. Marie Chen, eleven. He read it twice, then scrolled down and found no one else. The customers who had ordered nothing were not hiding at the bottom of the list. They had simply vanished.

Nico, over video call from two time zones away, was no help at first. "So some people didn't order," Nico said, chewing something. "Who cares." Evan cared, mostly because his grandfather had spent ten minutes explaining that a man named Harold Ostergaard had come into the shop every winter for nine years, complained about the price of granite, and never once bought a slab. "He was an epicure of other people's merchandise," his grandfather had said. "Tell me if the machine can find him."

Evan tried joining the tables in the other direction, Orders first and Customers second, and got the same forty-one rows in a different order. He understood then that an ordinary join kept only what matched, like a teacher taking attendance by calling only the names of students who answered. The silent ones stayed uncounted. He sat back and looked at his grandfather's kitchen, at the igneous chunks of countertop sample propped by the window, rock that had cooled from something molten into something useful, and he thought about direction. Whichever table came first, the join seemed to favor it. So what would happen if one table came first and the join were required, for once, to be unfair?

He typed LEFT JOIN where he had typed JOIN before, Customers on the left. He ran it, not beseeching the machine exactly, though it felt close to that. The list came back with fifty-three rows. There they were: the forty-one customers, and below them twelve more, each with a name and phone number and, where the order columns should have been, the word NULL, repeated in gray, like a chair pulled out for someone who never sat down. Harold Ostergaard was the fourth row. Nine years of visits, and the machine summed his lifetime of purchases as nothing at all.

Mr. Francis, the neighbor who repaired clocks and had somehow become Evan's grandfather's chess partner, wandered in for the evening game and looked over Evan's shoulder. "LEFT JOIN," Evan said, pointing at the screen, since that was what the words on the page said. Mr. Francis put on his glasses, studied the NULLs, and said only, "Your grandmother's in there twice." She was. Carol M., entered as a customer in her own right in 1987 and again as a co-signer on two of her husband's orders, sat in the list both as a buyer and as a blank. The machine was honest about her, which was more than Evan could decide to be.

Because here was what he could not resolve: the list called those twelve people customers who had never ordered, and that was true, but his grandfather's notebooks called some of them friends, and one of them a wife, and one of them, scrawled beside a 1994 phone number in different ink, "do not call again." A person could be present in one ledger and absent from another without either ledger being wrong. Evan understood the join now, both directions of it, which table kept every row and which one went blank where nothing matched. What he did not know was which direction his grandfather would want to read the answer from, or whether a man who kept paper notebooks for thirty years wanted the truth of it flattened into rows at all.

He printed the list anyway, fifty-three lines, and carried it to the porch where his grandfather sat waiting with the chessboard already set. Evan put the page beside the captured pawns, and his grandfather found Harold Ostergaard's name without being told, and read it twice, and tapped the NULL beside it with one finger. "So the machine says nothing," his grandfather said. "Nine years." He looked out toward the darkening road, then moved a pawn forward two squares and said, "Your move."

activity: to compare two apartment leases and work out the total monthly cost including utilities
knowledge_domain: to compare two apartment leases and work out the total monthly cost including utilities
fact: Electricity is billed by the kilowatt-hour, so using 600 kilowatt-hours at 15 cents each costs 90 dollars, before any fixed monthly charges.
story:
Kellan had commandeered the folding table with his architecture portfolio before Levi even got his first load in, so Levi spread the two leases across the lid of a washer three machines down and told himself it didn't matter, that the light was better here anyway. It wasn't. The fluorescent above him flickered every few seconds like something moribund, and both leases were printed in a font so small he had to tilt each page toward the window to read the fine print at all.

"You're doing it wrong," Kellan called over, not looking up from his drawings. "You're reading them like they're going to tell you the answer. They're not. They're built to hide it."

"I didn't ask," Levi said, but he said it without heat, because Kellan had a way of being right about the wrong things, and because Levi had been on the same line for ten minutes without absorbing a word of it. The first apartment, the one on Delmore Street, was six hundred a month plus utilities. The second, above the dry cleaner where Iyad's cousin had lived, was six eighty with heat and water included but electricity separate. He was seventeen, he had a bank statement and two paychecks from the greenhouse, and a deadline of Friday, and his mother's voice in his head saying if you're going to do this, do it properly, which he had chosen to hear as permission rather than worry, though he suspected it was mostly worry.

Iyad came in carrying his laundry in a duffel bag he never actually opened, which Levi had noticed before and never asked about, because Iyad's real reason for coming to the laundromat was clearly the company and everyone let it stand. "Delmore's got the better light," Iyad said, dropping onto the counter beside Levi. "Big windows facing west. The dry cleaner place smells like starch, all day, forever."

"You'd pay forty a month extra for light?"

"Absolutely. I'm an aesthete, Levi. Some of us care about beauty." Iyad said it grandly, mocking himself even as he said it, which was how he said most things.

Levi turned back to the leases and did what he had not thought to do yet, which was call the number on the Delmore listing and simply ask. The landlord sounded old and unhurried. When Levi asked what the previous tenant usually paid for electricity, the man said he'd have to check, then came back and said the bills ran about six hundred kilowatt-hours a month. Levi wrote it on the margin of the lease, the units and everything, because he didn't know what else to do with them.

"What's a kilowatt-hour get you," Kellan said, and it wasn't really a question, it was Kellan being Kellan.

Ms. Adebayo, who ran the flower shop next door and did her wash here on Tuesday nights, was loading the machine beside his. "Fifteen cents each, here, before the service charge," she said mildly, shaking a pillowcase out. "It's on the back of your bill if you read the back."

Levi looked at his margin. Six hundred kilowatt-hours. Fifteen cents each. He did it in his head first and then on paper because he didn't trust his head: six hundred times fifteen cents, ninety dollars, and that was before whatever fixed monthly charge the bill added on top. So Delmore was six hundred plus ninety plus the unknown service charge plus water, which the lease said was billed separately and which he had no number for at all. He added it anyway, penciling a plus sign and a blank, and the total crept past seven hundred and kept climbing into spaces he hadn't budgeted. The dry cleaner place was six eighty and done, mostly. He sat with both pages side by side and understood, for the first time in a way that had numbers attached, that the cheaper-looking apartment was probably the more expensive one, and that he still couldn't be sure, because of the water.

He told himself he'd take the second one. He told Iyad this, out loud, folding a shirt he'd actually washed while Iyad's duffel sat untouched, and Iyad looked genuinely wounded about the starch smell, and Kellan said the dry cleaner building was a bad building, he'd seen it, the lint in the vents alone, and Levi noticed that both of them wanted him to choose the other apartment, each for his own reasons, and that he had already stopped listening to either of them, which felt like growing up and also like losing something he couldn't name in the flickering light.

He went out to the pay phone by the door and called the Delmore landlord back, asked him what water usually ran, and the man said it varied. Levi wrote that down too, the word varied, and underlined it twice.

"Friday," Iyad called from inside. "You said Friday. It's Tuesday."

"I know what day it is," Levi said, and he did, and he stood by the phone a moment longer, one lease folded in each back pocket like two different futures, and then went back in to move his load to the dryer.

activity: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
knowledge_domain: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
fact: The Situation-Behavior-Impact model, from the Center for Creative Leadership, frames feedback by naming when it happened, what the person did, and what effect it had.
story:
The porch swing at her grandmother's house had a specific complaint, a squeak on every third pump of the legs, and Hailey had learned over three summers of visits that the trick was to time your rocking so the squeak landed on the offbeat, where it sounded almost intentional. She was working on this when Elisa texted her the seventh draft of the same paragraph, with a message that said only: be brutal.

Hailey did not want to be brutal. She wanted to be honest, which was turning out to be a different and harder thing. She and Elisa ran the school's literary magazine together, and in two weeks they would have to sit across from contributors and tell thirty teenagers what was and wasn't working in their poems. Last spring, Hailey had told a boy on her soccer team that his passing was lazy, and she had watched his face close like a shop shutter. She had meant one bad decision in the second half, a through ball he didn't chase, but what he heard was a verdict on his whole character. She thought about that a lot, the way the words had traveled and arrived somewhere she hadn't aimed.

She typed "it's fine" and deleted it. She typed "the ending feels rushed" and deleted that too, because what did rushed even ask Elisa to do? Inside the house, her grandmother was being a taciturn audience for the radio, stirring something on the stove and offering no commentary to either. Hailey went in to get tea, and on the kitchen table, half buried under seed catalogs, she found a workbook her grandfather must have left before he died: a leadership training manual from some course he'd taken at the plant. She flipped through it out of curiosity, the way you open a stranger's diary if the stranger is family.

There it was, on a page with his pencil marks in the margin. A model called Situation-Behavior-Impact, from something called the Center for Creative Leadership. She read it twice. You named when it happened, then what the person actually did, then the effect it had. No adjectives about anyone's soul. Next to a sample script, her grandfather had written, in his blunt hand, "finally a way to talk to Doug." Hailey laughed out loud, then covered her mouth, because she had never met Doug but felt she knew exactly what Doug had been doing to him for thirty years. Her grandmother looked over, saw the page, and almost smiled. "He practiced that thing in the mirror," she said. "On the mirror, actually. Talked to his own reflection like it owed him money." Hailey tried to picture it, her grandfather, a man so economical with praise that he once called her state championship trophy "not bad," rehearsing kindness on a piece of glass, and something about the image made her chest go tight and warm at once.

She took her tea back to the swing. On the third pump, the squeak. She opened Elisa's paragraph again, which was about a drowned town, and this time she tried to watch her own thinking the way the manual had taught her grandfather to watch Doug's. First the situation: the last four sentences of the piece. Then the behavior: Elisa switched from the flooded church to her narrator's mother packing a car, with no bridge between them. Then the impact: Hailey had to read it three times, and each time she lost the ache the church had built. She tried writing it that way, sentence by sentence, and something strange happened. The honesty got sharper, not softer, because she had to be precise instead of vague, and it got kinder, not crueler, because there was nothing in it about Elisa, only about the page.

But then she stopped, phone in her lap, because a doubt arrived that the workbook hadn't covered. Elisa had asked to be eviscerated, in those exact words, on draft two, and had seemed disappointed when Hailey held back. Maybe some people wanted the wound because it felt like proof the reader had fought with the work. Maybe precision, with its careful scaffolding of when and what and effect, would read to Elisa like a lawyer's letter. Or maybe that was just Hailey looking for an excuse to stay vague. She genuinely could not tell which it was, and she noticed that she didn't mind not knowing, that the not knowing felt like the beginning of the skill rather than the failure of it.

Suri called at nine, from her house two streets over, wanting to know if Hailey had seen the group chat. "Elisa's spiraling," Suri said. "She thinks you hated it because you didn't answer for two hours." Hailey looked at the message she'd drafted, and at the dark yard, and at the swing chain still swaying faintly from her last rock. She pressed call instead of send on Elisa's number, and put the phone to her ear, and heard it pick up on the first ring.

"Before you apologize for existing," Hailey said, "read me your last four sentences out loud."

activity: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
knowledge_domain: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
fact: Sociologist Mark Granovetter's 1973 paper 'The Strength of Weak Ties' found that people often learned of new jobs through acquaintances rather than close friends.
story:
The house smelled like paint and nothing else, which Emile understood was the smell of a life not yet lived in. His parents had driven back to the old city to collect the second trailer load, leaving him with a sleeping bag, a phone at forty percent, and instructions to wait for the Internet installer sometime between one and five. He walked the bare rooms in his socks and tried to decide which one would be his, though the choice had already been made for him, the small one over the garage, and the deciding was only a way of pretending he still had a hand in things.

On the kitchen counter, where a note from his mother said there were granola bars in the blue box, his phone buzzed. Jaskaran. Miss u already loser. Then, a minute later, something longer. My uncle was telling us about this sociologist, Granovetter, 1973, paper called the strength of weak ties. He found people mostly learned about new jobs through acquaintances, not close friends. Kind of messed up if u think about it.

Emile sat down on the floor with his back against the island and read it twice. He was tempted to introspect about why this bothered him, the suggestion that the people he loved were, statistically speaking, useless to him, but he didn't like the word even inside his own head; it sounded like something you did instead of doing something. He typed back, Cool story, and then deleted it, and then typed, Tell Lucian the empty house has an echo. He recorded himself shouting Lucian's name into the stairwell and sent the file. The echo was genuinely impressive.

Through the window over the sink he saw a woman in the neighbouring garden, cutting back a rose bush with the unhurried violence of someone who had done it every year for decades. She caught him looking and raised the shears in a small salute. He had met her once, briefly, on the day his parents signed the papers: Ms. Traoré, from next door, who had said the previous owners were decent enough but kept a virulent compost pile nobody would miss. He went to the front door before he could talk himself out of it.

"You're the boy who arrived before the furniture," she said. Not a question. She was holding a foil-covered dish, which she explained was her welcome-to-the-street lasagna, and which she did not hand over until he had agreed to come in from the doorway, because, she said, only vampires and salesmen conduct conversations on thresholds. Inside her kitchen there were cookbooks stacked like masonry and a cat that inspected him at ankle height and found him acceptable.

She asked what he was planning to do with himself in a town he had seen for a total of nine hours. He said he didn't know yet. He was aware that this was the sort of question adults asked in order to hand you an answer, and he was curious which answer she was holding.

"My brother runs the bookshop on Alder Street," she said. "He's short a pair of hands on Saturdays now that school's started. It's real work, boxes and the register, not much glamour." She sliced the lasagna and gave him a plate as if the job and the food were the same transaction. "I could mention you."

He thought of Jaskaran's text, and of Lucian, whose father had spent three months asking around at his own office before finding Emile's one previous job, a summer of shelving at a library nobody shopped at. All that effort, all those strong ties, and here was a woman he had spoken to exactly twice, offering him employment over carbohydrates. "A friend just told me about that," he said. "Granovetter. The strength of weak ties."

She looked at him with an interest she hadn't shown before, the discernment of someone who sorted people by what they read. "Then you'll take the job, since you already know how these things work." It wasn't quite a question either.

The installer never came, and when his parents rolled in at dusk with the trailer, his mother asked how his day had been and he said, "I got a job," and watched her set down a box to look at him properly. In his room over the garage, which still had no bed and no curtain, he lay in the sleeping bag and wrote to Jaskaran: ur uncle is right. Got a job today from the neighbor. Met her twice. Lucian replied with a single string of exclamation points, and then, a few minutes later, does that mean we're not going to find you a better one. Emile looked at the message for a long time, the streetlight striping the bare floor through the uncurtained window, and typed, no it means you're off the hook, and left it unsent, his thumb hovering over the blue arrow, the house ticking and settling around him in the dark.

activity: to lead a holiday meal ceremony from start to finish for the whole family
knowledge_domain: to lead a holiday meal ceremony from start to finish for the whole family
fact: The Haggadah is the book read aloud at a Passover Seder; it retells the story of the Israelites' exodus from slavery in Egypt.
story:
Antoine found the box of Haggadot in his grandmother's hallway closet on the morning of the Seder, wedged behind the vacuum cleaner like something nobody had wanted to think about since last spring. There were eleven copies, wine-ringed and soft at the corners, and he counted them twice because his grandfather had said, on the phone, "You're leading this year, so you count the books." That was all he'd said. Not how, not in what order, not what to do when his uncle inevitably started arguing before the soup.

"You're doing the whole thing?" Rayan had asked him in the parking lot on Thursday, hauling recycling bins for Ms. Ho's fundraiser drive. "Like, start to finish?" Antoine had shrugged, and Ms. Ho, overhearing, had said only, "My mother led ours once when my father was ill. She said the book does most of the work if you let it." He hadn't asked what book. He'd nodded as though he already knew, which was, he was beginning to understand, a habit of his.

Now, at the kitchen table, he spread the copies out. His grandfather arrived at four with a cane nobody had mentioned on the phone, sat down heavily, and tapped the top copy with one finger. "You know what that is," he said. It wasn't a question, but it required an answer anyway.

"The Haggadah," Antoine said. "It's the book we read aloud at the Seder. It retells the story of the Israelites leaving slavery in Egypt."

His grandfather looked at him for a long moment. "Your grandmother would have liked to hear you say that." Then he ate a radish and refused to elaborate.

The trouble began with the seating. His uncle's girlfriend had never been to a Seder; his cousin Dara, fourteen and recently pugnacious about every tradition on earth, had announced she wasn't reading anything she hadn't personally vetted; and his mother was still at the stove, steam fogging her glasses, saying "Whatever you decide, Antoine, it's your table," in the tone of someone testing whether that was true. Antoine had assumed leading meant performing, the way his grandfather had, voice like a cantor's, everyone's eyes down. Sitting there with eleven books and thirteen chairs, he understood it meant something closer to distributing. If the Haggadah retold the exodus aloud, then the table had to share it out, and how he divided the passages decided who felt included and who felt like an audience.

He did it unevenly on purpose. Short passages to the girlfriend, in English. The Four Questions to the youngest kid, who'd been rehearsing in the bathroom all afternoon; Antoine could hear him through the door, stopping and restarting, furious at his own voice. To Dara he gave the section about the wicked son, handed it over without comment, and Dara, who had been ready to denigrate the whole enterprise as theater, read it with sudden, careful attention, and looked up afterward as if Antoine had seen something in her she hadn't planned to show.

Halfway through, his uncle started in about politics, and Antoine, instead of waiting him out the way his grandfather always had, let him run for one full minute and then said, "There's a passage about that, actually," and assigned him the section on the wise son. It was a gamble. Rihanna, his study partner, had told him once that the ascetic approach to family conflict, silence, denial, the clean fast, never worked for her house; you had to feed the argument something. His uncle read, grumbled, and stayed at the table, which Antoine counted as a win.

The twist came near the end. When they reached the final songs, his grandfather pulled Antoine aside by the coat closet and pressed something into his hand: a photocopied page, folded into quarters, covered in handwriting Antoine recognized from birthday cards. "Your grandmother's commentary," his grandfather said. "She wrote it for the year she was going to lead. I was going to do it that year. Then she got sick, and I kept using her page without telling anyone whose words they were." He paused. "Read it tonight or don't. But it's yours now."

Antoine unfolded it at the table, in front of everyone, because hiding it felt like the old way. The handwriting was shaky in places, firm in others. It said, among other things, that the exodus story was told aloud, every single year, not because anyone would forget it but because a story read only in silence belongs to no one, and a story passed around the table, voice by voice, belongs to everyone at it. Dara leaned over his shoulder to read. The girlfriend asked, "Can I read that part out loud?" and Antoine said, "It's yours," and slid the page down the table.

He didn't know if he'd led it well, or whether his grandfather's silence during the reading was approval or grief, or whether next year would fall to him again. That could stay unknown. His grandfather raised his cup when the last song ended, looked straight at him, and said, "Same time next year, leader."

activity: going on a first date
knowledge_domain: going on a first date
fact: In a 1966 experiment by Elliot Aronson and colleagues, a highly competent quiz contestant who spilled a cup of coffee was rated more likable afterward; this is called the pratfall effect.
story:
Aaron had read the psychology chapter twice before Bronwyn agreed to dinner, and by six o'clock he could recite the relevant experiment in his head: in 1966, Elliot Aronson and some colleagues had shown that a highly competent quiz contestant who spilled a cup of coffee was rated more likable afterward. It was called the pratfall effect. He wasn't sure yet how the information would be useful, but he liked having it.

The date was at his house because his mother had insisted, and because cooking for someone felt less like a performance than a restaurant would. She had left for the evening with a shopping bag and a warning not to malign the lasagne before he tasted it. Bronwyn arrived at seven in a green jacket, holding a bottle of sparkling cider she'd bought from the cashier at the corner shop who had carded her anyway.

"Your house smells like a bakery," she said.

"It's the cheese. It's been in there since four."

They ate at the kitchen table because the dining room felt like a holiday. She asked about the psychology elective, and he told her about Mr. Chaudhry's habit of pacing the front of the room with the projector remote in his hand like a conductor's baton. She asked whether any of it was true or whether it was all just studies on college sophomores who needed course credit. He said that was a fair question and then, before he could stop himself, he reached for his water glass and knocked it into her lap.

The glass did not break. The water went everywhere else. It soaked the front of her jeans and ran off the table onto her sneakers, and Aaron sat there with his hand still shaped around air where the glass had been.

"I'm so sorry," he said. "That's it, the whole evening's ruined. I've killed it in the first twenty minutes."

Bronwyn stood up, holding her sleeves away from the wet. "It's water. It dries." But her voice had gone flat, and she took the dish towel he offered without looking at him.

He filled the kettle for no reason other than that his hands wanted a task. And it was there, at the counter, that the chapter surfaced whole: the competent contestant, the coffee, 1966, Aronson. The spilling had made the contestant more likable, not less. He turned around.

"Okay, this is going to sound like an excuse," he said. "It's not. In 1966 this researcher, Elliot Aronson, and his colleagues ran an experiment. A quiz contestant who was really competent spills a cup of coffee, and afterward people rated him as more likable. It's called the pratfall effect."

Bronwyn sat down slowly, still holding the towel. "You knocked a drink on me and now you're citing sources."

"I'm telling you why I'm not panicking."

"You should be panicking a little. My shoes are squelching."

He set the kettle down. "The contestant was competent first. That's the part that matters. The spill only helped because people already thought he was good. If a mediocre contestant spilled, he just looked worse. So I can't actually use this. I don't know which one I am yet. You don't either. We've known each other for one movie night and a chemistry lab."

She looked at her shoes, then at him, and something shifted in her face, the way a held breath lets itself out. "That's the most honest thing anyone's said to me on a first date," she said. "Most people just apologize until you forgive them to make it stop."

"I can do that too. I can do both."

They moved to the living room, where the cushions were ductile in a way the kitchen chairs weren't, and she told him about her father's habit of tracing every stubborn streak of temper back through the family lineage as if it were an inheritance he could audit. Aaron said his mother did something similar with grudges. Outside, a neighbor's dog barked twice and stopped. Later, when she was pulling on her jacket at the door, still faintly damp, she paused with her hand on the zipper.

"So if Wilson tells everyone at school you dumped water on me," she said, "what do I say?"

"Tell them Aronson said it makes me more likable." He held the door. "Then tell them I spilled it, which is the part that's actually true."

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: Robert Cialdini's 1976 study found that students wore more university clothing after their football team won and said 'we' more when describing wins than losses.
story:
The rink smelled of cold rubber and burnt coffee, and Audrey had claimed the end of the bench nearest the glass so that her breath fogged a small circle on the pane whenever she leaned forward. Her father sat to her left with his gloves in his lap, still wearing them, which he did at every game as if the cold might otherwise desiccate his hands into something useless. To her right, Mahi had her boots up on the rail, and Gabriel had arrived late, flustered, in the university hoodie his uncle had mailed him in September.

On the ice, the home team was down by one with six minutes left. Audrey knew most of the players from years of early mornings in this same building, back when she still carried her own skates in a bag with a broken zipper. She had quit at fourteen, and she had told herself the reasons so often they had gone smooth and hard, like a stone she kept in her pocket. Her brother was the one who stayed. He was on the second line tonight, and every time he came over the boards her father's gloves clenched in his lap.

The tying goal came off a rebound, and the building made the sound Audrey remembered from the inside, that roar that seemed to come up through the soles of your feet. Mahi grabbed her arm. Gabriel stood up with both fists in the air, and when the home team scored again thirty seconds later, empty net, the last two minutes all jagged relief, Gabriel turned around to the whole row of strangers behind them and held up one finger.

"We won," he said. "We actually won."

Audrey was grinning too, and then, somewhere between the grin and the next breath, she heard the word. She had read something once, in a paperback her mother had bought at a library sale, its provenance a mystery since no one in the house studied psychology. She'd read it on the bus in October, half attending, half watching the rain. She dug in her backpack now, past the granola bars, and found it with a receipt still marking the page.

"You wore that hoodie all week," Mahi said to Gabriel. "You've never played a game in your life."

"Faith," Gabriel said. "It's called faith."

"Last Tuesday you said the team was an embarrassment to the town."

Audrey held up the book. "Listen. In 1976 there was this study. Robert Cialdini. After the football team won, students wore more university clothing than after losses. And when they described the wins, they said 'we' more. When they described the losses, they said 'we' less." She read it again to be sure she had it right, and she had, both parts, the clothing and the pronoun.

"So I'm a lab result," Gabriel said, but he said it quietly, looking down at the logo on his chest.

"No," Audrey said. "It's not like that. It's not a trick you fell for." And she wasn't sure that was true either, which was the part she kept turning over as the crowd funneled up the stairs around them and the Zamboni came out to do its slow, indifferent laps. She wanted to say that belonging was real even when it borrowed its evidence from a scoreboard, that the "we" was a kind of promise rather than a claim, but she could hear how it would sound, a speech in a cold corridor, so she didn't say it.

Outside, the parking lot was full of exhaust and shouting kids, their breath evanescent in the floodlights, there and gone. Mahi's mother was honking from the far row. Gabriel pulled the hood up over his hair, and Audrey noticed that her father was saying "we" too, to another father, "we really buried them in the third," and her father had also never played, had never even skated, and no one would ever call him out on it.

Her brother came out last with his bag over one shoulder, hair wet, and he stopped when he saw them, and his tired face did something complicated. Audrey felt the "we" rise in her own mouth and held it there. She had earned nothing tonight. She had sat on a bench. And yet when he lifted his chin at her, that look that went back to backyard nets and broken zippers, the word didn't feel stolen. It felt like a door she had never fully closed.

"Next week," her brother said, "could you maybe come to the early one. The Sunday one. Nobody comes to the Sunday ones."

She had told herself she left because the mornings were brutal and the game had stopped mattering, and she had also told herself, on worse nights, that she left because she wasn't good enough, and the truth had a shape she still couldn't see whole. Maybe the study was about vanity, she thought, and maybe it was about something closer to love, and maybe there was no clean line between the two, and she was sixteen and the book was a library-sale paperback and she didn't know yet.

"Okay," she said. "The Sunday one."

Gabriel, walking backward toward Mahi's mother's car, called out, "You better wear the hoodie," and she looked down at her plain coat and laughed, and Mahi pulled her toward the car by the sleeve.

activity: to compare how a parliamentary and a presidential system choose and remove a head of government
knowledge_domain: to compare how a parliamentary and a presidential system choose and remove a head of government
fact: In 1982 Helmut Kohl replaced Helmut Schmidt as German chancellor through a constructive vote of no confidence, the only time the procedure has succeeded at the federal level.
story:
The library smelled of radiator dust and old glue, and the clock above the reference shelf ticked louder than it should have. Violet spread her notes across the table: two columns, one headed PARLIAMENTARY, one PRESIDENTIAL, and beneath the headings, mostly blank space. The debate assignment was due Thursday, and she had drawn Imogen as a partner, which meant she had drawn the actual work as well.

"Tell me again why this matters," Imogen said, dropping into the chair across from her, hair still damp from gym.

"Because Ms. Koné says half our class thinks every country votes the way we do." Violet tapped the presidential column. "You vote for a president, the president serves the term, and short of impeachment, that's it. Nobody in the middle can just swap them out."

"Sounds tidy."

"It is tidy. That's the problem with it." She wasn't sure why she'd said that, and Imogen raised an eyebrow, so she pushed on. "The other system isn't tidy. The parliament picks the head of government, and the parliament can un-pick them."

Imogen pulled out her phone. "So give me one time it actually happened. A real one, not a diagram."

Violet had the library's Germany volume open already, because she'd pulled it more or less at random, and she was running her finger down the index under K when Imogen asked. Kohl, Helmut. She turned to the page and read it twice.

"Okay," she said slowly. "Germany. 1982. Helmut Kohl replaced Helmut Schmidt as chancellor." She looked up. "And there was no election. The Bundestag just did it."

"Did what? Fired him?"

"It's called a constructive vote of no confidence." She said the phrase carefully, the way she'd read it, and watched Imogen frown at the word constructive as though it had betrayed her.

"That's an odd word for getting rid of somebody."

"That's the point, though." Violet copied the year into her parliamentary column, her pen pressing hard enough to dent the page. "They didn't just say we hate Schmidt, goodbye. They had to name a replacement first. Kohl. So the country was never headless, and the voters never went to the polls." She checked the page again. "It's the only time it's worked at the federal level. They've got the procedure on the books, and in all those decades, it succeeded that once."

Imogen leaned over and read the paragraph herself, lips moving slightly. "So the voters elected Schmidt, sort of, and then got Kohl instead, and nobody asked them."

"That's the ugly version, yeah."

"That's the version I'd argue."

Violet sat back. The radiator clanked; somewhere behind the stacks, a scanner beeped and stopped. She had planned to argue the presidential side herself, actually, the tidy side, the side where a mandate means something. She'd been fairly sanguine about it at lunch, telling Emerik it would be an easy win, and Emerik had laughed at her and said nothing was an easy win with Imogen on the other team.

"Here's what's bothering me," Violet said. "With the president, you get stability, but you also get stuck. Four years with somebody the whole legislature despises, everybody watching the clock. With the parliament, you get responsiveness, but a majority can change the leader by its own volition, no voters required, and 1982 is the proof it can happen." She slid the book across. "Both of those are real. Both of them cost something."

"So pick one and lambaste the other. That's what debates are."

"No, that's what bad debates are." She took the book back. "Ms. Koné keeps saying a considered position isn't the same as a confident one."

Imogen rolled her eyes, but she pulled out a pen and started writing in the margin of her own notebook, which was more than she'd done all week. "Fine. You take the middle and I'll take the attacks. Split the work."

They worked until the librarian began clicking off the bank of lights by the windows, and the long table went from bright to dim in stages, like something deciding. Violet found herself reading the Kohl page a third time, not for facts now but for the shape of it. A chancellor gone, a chancellor installed, an entire machinery of government turning over in an afternoon while the electorate watched from the outside. It unsettled her in a way she couldn't quite file under either column.

On Thursday the classroom smelled of whiteboard marker and somebody's strawberry deodorant. Ms. Koné stood at the sideboard with her arms folded while pairs went up front. When their turn came, Imogen argued first, crisp and ruthless, painting the parliamentary maneuver as a loophole, a backdoor, leadership changed without a single ballot cast. Violet stepped up after her, hands flat on the podium, and felt the class waiting for her to demolish her partner.

"Imogen's right that no election happened," Violet said. "In 1982 Kohl replaced Schmidt as German chancellor through a constructive vote of no confidence, and that's the only time the procedure has succeeded at the federal level. No general election, no say for the voters. That's the cost." She paused. "Now hold that next to the presidential side, where a leader can sit through a full term that most of the legislature wants to end, and the voters can't do anything either, except wait. Both systems take power away from somebody. I think the parliamentary version is more honest about it, but I can't prove that. I can only show you the one time it happened."

Ms. Koné uncrossed her arms. Emerik, third row, mouthed the word "sanguine" at her with a grin, and Violet ignored him.

After the bell, Ms. Koné caught her at the door. "You left it open at the end," she said.

"I know," said Violet. "I couldn't close it and still be telling the truth."

Ms. Koné wrote something small in her grade book, and Violet walked out into the corridor with the loose pages still warm from her hands.

activity: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
knowledge_domain: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
fact: The 1967 Holmes and Rahe stress scale lists a change in residence as a stressful life event worth 20 points, the same as a change in schools.
story:
The moving truck had left at dawn, and by noon the family car was alone on the highway with three suitcases in the back and Aaron in the passenger seat holding a box he refused to let go into the truck. Inside it were the things he had not trusted to strangers: a fossil ammonite Kimberly had given him for his birthday, and the photocopied packet from Mr. Villanueva's psychology elective, which he had shoved in at the last minute because it happened to be on his desk.

"You could put that on your lap instead of hugging it," his mother said. "You look like you're guarding state secrets."

"I am." He set the box down but kept one hand on it.

They stopped for gas outside a town whose name he had never heard before and would, apparently, now learn to pronounce. While his mother stood at the pump, Aaron's phone buzzed: a photo from Joaquin of the empty spot in the school parking lot where the three of them used to park, captioned "they expropriated your space already. Some junior with a lifted truck." Aaron wrote back "tell him it's cursed" and then, because that was a lie he didn't feel like maintaining, deleted it and sent nothing.

At the next rest stop, stretched out on a picnic table under a canopy of oaks, he opened Mr. Villanueva's packet to look like he was doing summer work. The chapter was on stress. He was skimming, half his attention on the phone, when he stopped at a table of life events with numbers beside them. He read it twice, then took out a pen and drew a line connecting two rows.

When his mother came back with two bottles of water, he held the page up. "In 1967 two psychologists, Holmes and Rahe, made a stress scale. A change in residence is worth 20 points."

"So?"

"The same as a change in schools. Same exact number." He tapped the page. "I'm doing both. At the same time."

She sat down across from him and looked at the table upside down, squinting. "That's forty points of what?"

"Stress. It counts it like a real thing. Like an injury." He heard his own voice climb and brought it down. "I thought I was just being weak about it. Moving. You keep saying it's an adventure."

Her jaw tightened the way it did when his father's name came up in certain tones. "I keep saying that because somebody in this car has to." She unscrewed her water, took a drink, and looked at the highway instead of at him. He understood, suddenly, that her insouciance was a job she performed, the way he performed not caring in front of Joaquin, and that both performances had costs. He also understood that this did not make the moving easier, only the loneliness of it slightly less private.

"Kimberly texted me a phylogeny joke," he said, after a while. "She heard I actually read the packet."

"Which is what?"

"Something about how my stress scale should show common ancestry with every other teenager who ever got dragged across a state line. It's funnier at three in the morning." He turned the phone over in his hands. The screen showed her message from an hour ago, unanswered: "Call when you land. Or don't. But call." Her want was as plain as the punctuation. She wanted him to promise something, and he had spent two weeks not promising anything, because a promise felt like agreeing that the distance was survivable, and he wasn't sure yet whether it was.

He got up, walked to the far side of the rest area where the traffic noise was louder, and dialed. She answered before the first ring finished.

"I'm not there yet," he said. "Two more hours."

"I know. Your mom's location thing is still shared with me."

"So you've been watching me drive all morning and you waited until now."

"I was doing the 20 points too," she said. "One text per rest stop. Pacing myself."

He laughed, and it came out rougher than he meant it to. He looked back toward the table, where his mother was folding the map she never needed because the phone did it for her, keeping her hands busy, and he turned away and said, "When I get there, I'll figure out the phone plan. Nights are yours."

"Nights are yours too," Kimberly said, and he could hear Joaquin in the background shouting something about the cursed parking spot.

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: A 1985 study by Thomas Gilovich, Robert Vallone and Amos Tversky concluded that basketball shooters' streaks were no more common than chance, calling the 'hot hand' a fallacy.
story:
The playoff game was in two days, and Luke's backyard had become the team's whole world. His father had poured the slab behind the garage years ago, and the portable hoop's base had cracked and been filled with sand, so the rim shook after every shot like something deciding whether to agree. Six of them ran three-on-three until the mosquitoes came up from the creek, shirts stuck to their backs, the porch light making a small yellow republic of court in the dark.

Luke had made five shots in a row when Celia called for the ball and then, unaccountably, didn't shoot. She stood at the top of the key holding the ball with both hands, staring past him.

"Give it back to Luke," she said to Isabela, who was open under the rim. "He's five for five."

Isabela didn't move. "I'm right here."

"He's hot," Celia said. "You don't take the ball from the hot man."

The play collapsed, everyone shouting, and Luke ended up taking a contested fadeaway that clanked off the back rim so hard the whole hoop shuddered. They argued about it through two water breaks and into the next game. Celia had a whole theory about momentum, about how a shooter's confidence rose like a tide and you rode it. She wasn't trying to denigrate Isabela's game; she honestly believed she was coaching. But Isabela had gone quiet in a way Luke recognized from school, the way people went quiet when they'd been told, however gently, that they were the wrong choice.

That night Luke lay on his bed with his phone on his chest, not searching for anything, until he thought about what Celia had said and typed it in almost as a joke. He found it fast. A 1985 study by Thomas Gilovich, Robert Vallone and Amos Tversky had looked at basketball shooters and concluded that streaks were no more common than chance. They'd called the hot hand a fallacy. He read the sentence three times. Then he read it aloud to his ceiling, because it felt like the kind of thing that needed air.

The next practice was the last one before the game, and Luke came to the backyard early, while the light was still long and gold across the slab. He brought his notebook, which the team mocked him for, calling him a connoisseur of pointless statistics. But he'd spent his study hall doing something that felt almost like cheating: he'd pulled up their own games, the ones his father filmed from the porch, and made a tally. After a teammate made three shots in a row, how did they do on the fourth? He'd counted. He'd made himself not round in anyone's favor.

When the others arrived, he tossed the notebook onto the folding chair by the fence.

"Celia," he said. "Question. If a guy hits three in a row, what are the odds he hits the fourth?"

"Way better than normal. He's feeling it."

"Because of a study, or because it looks that way?"

She dribbled the ball once, caught it, looked at him. "Because I've watched basketball my whole life."

"Okay. So in 1985 these researchers, Gilovich, Vallone and Tversky, they actually checked. Shooters' streaks were no more common than chance. The hot hand is a fallacy. That's the word they used."

"They said that? Who are they, gods?"

"They counted." He opened the notebook to the page with his tally, the pencil smudged where his palm had sweated on it. "And I counted us. After three makes in a row, our next shots went in about the same as always. Same as chance. All season."

Isabela took the notebook before Celia could. She read it standing under the rim, her lips moving slightly, and Luke watched her expression do something complicated: not triumph, which he'd half expected and half feared, but the slower look of a person rearranging furniture in a room.

"It's still three games," she said. "Small."

"Small," Luke agreed. "That's the part I keep snagging on. Their study was big. Mine's nothing. But it points the same direction."

Celia took the ball and personal-fouled a mosquito off her arm, which felt gratuitous, the slap echoing in the quiet yard. She walked to the top of the key and shot without warming up, and the ball went through clean, barely touching the rim, and the net made its small satisfied sound.

"So you're telling me that meant nothing," she said.

"I'm telling you the next one probably doesn't care about it."

They ran games until the light failed, and Celia kept passing to whoever was open instead of whoever was hot, which was Isabela a lot, and once was Luke, and once was nobody, the ball swinging around the perimeter until somebody had to decide. Luke played worse than usual, honestly, his mind snagging on the tally every time he touched the ball, wondering whether his own makes meant nothing or whether his wondering was itself a kind of curse. He didn't know. That was the strange gift of the whole evening: a thing could be measured, and the measuring could be true, and he could still stand at the free throw line with the porch light in his eyes not knowing what was about to happen.

Afterward, sitting on the porch steps with the last orange gone from the sky, Celia nudged his sneaker with hers.

"Tomorrow," she said, "when you get hot, I'm still giving you the ball."

"Not because of the study."

"Because you're my friend and it feels right." She stood, tucked the ball under her arm. "You can write that in your notebook."

Luke stayed on the steps a minute longer, listening to the creek, then got up and shot at the dark hoop, and the ball went somewhere he couldn't see.

activity: to critique a painting by Frida Kahlo using formal analysis of colour, composition and symbolism
knowledge_domain: to critique a painting by Frida Kahlo using formal analysis of colour, composition and symbolism
fact: In Self-Portrait with Thorn Necklace and Hummingbird, a black cat peers over Kahlo's shoulder, usually interpreted as a symbol of bad luck and death.
story:
The print of Kahlo's Self-Portrait with Thorn Necklace and Hummingbird had been taped to the pavilion wall with painter's tape, and by ten in the morning the lake behind it was so bright that the whole scene looked washed out, which was not the fault of the original, only of the light. Ms. Harper had given them until noon. Each of them had to stand up in front of the rest of the camp's art seminar and deliver a formal critique, meaning colour, composition, symbolism, and nothing about her bus accident, nothing about Diego, nothing about her feelings, which Ms. Harper called biography and treated like contraband.

Elijah had spent two evenings with the painting and had filled a legal pad with observations he did not trust. The palette was compressed: green foliage like a curtain, the artist's face in the middle plane, dead centre, frontal, unsmiling. The thorn necklace cut a horizontal line across her throat and drew a single bead of blood. There was a monkey on her right shoulder, tugging at the thorns. There was a butterfly pinned in her hair, iridescent and out of season. And behind her left shoulder, nearly hidden in the leaves, a black cat was watching the viewer with wide green eyes.

"You're being taciturn about it," Marianne said, dropping onto the bench beside him with her own notes, which were colour-coded. She said it like an accusation. "You've written one sentence about the cat."

"It's a cat," Elijah said.

"It's the cat," she said. "Miah went through the whole thing yesterday, animal by animal. Ask him."

Miah was at the far table arguing with a counsellor about whether a hummingbird could hover backwards, which it could, which had nothing to do with anything. When Elijah waved him over, Miah came reluctantly, still litigating over his shoulder. "The monkey is a pet from her real life, sure, whatever," Miah said, tapping the print. "The butterfly's a fragile thing, transformation, the usual. But the cat is the only animal in the whole painting looking out at us instead of at her. Black cat. Bad luck. Death, is the standard reading. Ms. Harper will say we can't just assert that, we have to show how the reading comes out of the form."

Elijah looked at the cat again. It was true that it alone met his eye, and true that the composition made it a dark shape against the foliage, a hole in the green. He had been planning to argue that the painting was about endurance, the stiff frontal pose, the thorns worn like jewellery. A dead hummingbird hanging from the necklace complicated that, and now the cat complicated it further. He wrote, in the margin, "endurance of what, exactly," and then crossed it out because it sounded like a question he was too tired to answer.

At eleven Ms. Harper rang the little brass bell and said the order would go by tables, so Elijah had roughly forty minutes, and Marianne, at his table, would go first. She stood and delivered a critique so clean it made his legal pad look like a ransom note: the foliage flattens the space, she said, so the figure is pushed forward, pressed against the surface of the picture the way the thorns press against her skin; the blood is the only warm red in the painting besides the flower, and it is tiny, and its smallness is the point. When she sat down, Ms. Harper said, "Good, though you didn't touch the animals," and Marianne looked at Elijah with an expression that said, your territory, take it.

He stood up with the pad and the print behind him and began with the symmetry, because that was solid ground: the monkey on the right shoulder and the cat on the left, dark shapes balancing each other, the face bisecting them like a fulcrum. Then he said the thing he had decided at the last minute to say, which was that the cat, in the standard reading, was a symbol of bad luck and death, but that he did not think the painting agreed with it, because the cat is the only animal looking at us, and the hummingbird, the dead thing at her throat, is the one she faces frontally, wearing it. The cat is off to the side, half in the leaves, almost an interruption. "She puts the death that's coming in the corner," he said, "and the death that's already happened around her neck."

There was a silence in the pavilion that he could not read, and then Miah said, "Or she keeps both where she can see them," and Ms. Harper, who had been writing, stopped writing. "That's the first sentence today I'd call a critique rather than a description," she said. "It's also unfalsifiable, which is a problem. But you found a way to hold the symbol and the composition together, which most of you did not, and you admitted you weren't sure, which counts for something. Not a grade. A something." She wrote a number on her clipboard that Elijah couldn't see from where he stood.

He sat down and Marianne nudged his pad toward the front of the table, where Ms. Harper was collecting them, and he realized the crossed-out question would be read by somebody, its veracity or its weakness judged in pencil in the margin. Outside, the noon whistle went off for swimming, and everyone surged toward the lake, and Miah hung back a second at the table. "The cat," he said. "For what it's worth, my grandmother says black cats are good luck. So Kahlo might have known that too." Then he ran to catch up with the others, and Elijah stood alone by the print, looking at the green eyes over the artist's shoulder, deciding whether to follow.

activity: to apply a feminist or Marxist critical lens to a passage from a classic novel
knowledge_domain: to apply a feminist or Marxist critical lens to a passage from a classic novel
fact: In Marxist terms, the bourgeoisie owns the means of production, such as factories and land, while the proletariat owns only its labour and must sell it for wages.
story:
The study room on the second floor of the public library smelled of dry-erase marker and someone else's coffee, and Brianna had commandeer ed the whiteboard an hour ago, which was longer than the little sign allowed but nobody had come to claim it. She had written two columns: OWNERS and WORKERS. Under OWNERS she had put Mr. Gradgrind, the mill owner Bounderby, and, after some hesitation, Mrs. Sparsit.
