Under WORKERS she had written only one name, Stephen Blackpool, and then a question mark, because she was not sure what to do with Sissy Jupe, who owned nothing and worked for no wages.

Axel arrived carrying the photocopied pages of Hard Times Ms. Aziz had left for them at the front desk, held together with a binder clip that had seen better decades. He read the whiteboard over her shoulder. "You're missing Louisa," he said.

"Louisa doesn't own anything."

"Louisa also doesn't work," Axel said, dropping into the chair beside her. "That's the point. She's not a worker and she can't own, because she's a woman. Her father trades her to Bounderby like she's a merger."

Brianna had not thought of it that way, and the not-thinking bothered her, because the whole reason she was here on a Saturday was the essay prompt Ms. Aziz had handed back with a single line in red pen: You summarize the plot; now tell me who has power and why. She could not fail that class. Not with the scholarship packet already in, not with her mother checking the mail each afternoon with a carefulness that pretended to be casual.

There was a flashback she kept returning to, from last spring. Ms. Aziz had kept her after the bell, not to scold her but to slide a paperback across the desk, a battered copy of some feminist criticism collection, and say, "You argue like someone who thinks the text is a window. Try thinking of it as a machine. Ask who built it and who has to run it." Brianna had carried the book around for weeks, understanding maybe a third of it, and had said thank you twice, which in retrospect was not enough.

Axel pulled the cap off the marker and stood at the board. "Okay, ground rules. In Marxist terms, the bourgeoisie owns the means of production. Factories, land, stuff like that. The proletariat owns only its labour, and has to sell it for wages." He drew a hard line under the two columns. "So sort them. Everybody in Coketown goes in one box or the other."

"That's the problem," Brianna said. "Louisa doesn't fit either box. And Sissy doesn't either, not really. She gets taken in, she doesn't get paid."

"Then maybe the boxes are the problem," Axel said, which was the kind of thing he said that sounded like wisdom and was usually just him being sullen about Victorian novels. But he said it while drawing a third column, wobbly, labelled DOESN'T FIT, and Brianna felt something shift in her chest, small and physical, like a door unsticking.

They worked through it together. Louisa in the third column, and underneath her Mrs. Sparsit again, because a widowed housekeeper with pretensions was neither owner nor wage-earner in any clean sense; and Rachael beside Stephen, and the question mark beside Sissy grew a second question mark. The feminist lens and the Marxist lens kept disagreeing, and Brianna found she liked the disagreement, that it made the novel feel less like a window and more like a machine with parts she could name. She wrote at the bottom of her notebook: the marriage market makes women a form of property the bourgeoisie passes between itself, which is litotes for slavery, more or less, and Ms. Aziz would probably strike the "more or less," but it was honest.

Taylor came in at four with three teas from the cart outside and no explanation for being an hour late, setting one down at Brianna's elbow without being asked, which was Taylor's way of apologizing. She read the third column, chewed her lip, and said, "So Dickens knew the boxes didn't fit and wrote the book anyway?"

"Or he didn't know," Axel said, "and the book knows more than he did."

Brianna looked at the board, at Louisa's name sitting outside both columns she had believed, an hour ago, could hold everyone. She picked up the eraser and held it against OWNERS, then moved it down and wiped out only the underline, leaving the words. Then her phone buzzed: Ms. Aziz, replying to the photo of the whiteboard Brianna had sent an hour before, back when she'd been proud of two columns. The message said, simply: Good start. Now erase the columns and tell me what Bounderby's mother gets for raising him.

"His mother," Brianna said aloud. Axel and Taylor both looked at the board, at all three columns, at the marker still in Axel's hand, and Taylor said, "Where does she go?"

activity: to compare how a parliamentary and a presidential system choose and remove a head of government
knowledge_domain: to compare how a parliamentary and a presidential system choose and remove a head of government
fact: Germany uses a constructive vote of no confidence: the Bundestag can remove a chancellor only by electing a successor in the same vote.
story:
The email from Mr. Farah-Ali arrived on the last Friday of summer: the first-year students would hold a mock parliament in the college's auditorium, and Chase, as newly elected leader of the fictional government, was expected to survive the session. His grandmother's house had the only quiet in the family that week, so he spread his notes across her kitchen table while she peeled apples and his grandfather watched the news channel with the volume too high. Kaiya had already texted him twice. You're going down first session, she wrote. Addison says he has the votes.

He had known Addison since seventh grade, which was exactly the problem. Addison knew that Chase's platform speech had gone over well but that the coalition behind it was a fragile thing, assembled out of people who liked winning more than they liked each other. In a presidential system, Chase thought, he would have a fixed term; they could hate him for four years and he would still sit there. Whatever this mock parliament was, it ran on parliamentary rules, and parliamentary rules meant the majority could reach up and pluck him off whenever it wanted. He wrote that in his notes, then crossed it out, because it felt like admitting he expected to lose.

His grandfather muted the television during a commercial and looked over at the papers. "You prognosticate too much," the old man said. "In my day we prepared for one fight, not ten." Chase said the fight was the same either way; the leader falls if the house turns. His grandfather shook his head once, the way he did when he thought something was wrong but not worth arguing, and turned the sound back on.

The screen was showing the German Bundestag. Footage of seats, a vote being counted, a man standing to accept the office. Chase watched without meaning to. Kaiya texted again: Addison's plan is a straight no-confidence vote on you, Monday morning, no candidate, just you gone. He typed back that it sounded clean, and then he stopped, because something about the German vote nagged at him, the way the successor appeared at the same moment the chancellor did not. He found his grandfather's old political encyclopedia on the shelf beside the clock and looked up the German terms until the entry gave him what he needed: a constructive vote of no confidence. The Bundestag can remove a chancellor only by electing a successor in the same vote.

He read it twice. Then he called Addison. "Your Monday plan," he said. "It wouldn't work in Germany. You can't just vote me out. You have to elect my replacement in the same vote." There was a pause on the line long enough to hear a television in the background. "So we'd have to agree on who comes next," Addison said slowly. "Before we pull the trigger." Chase said that was it exactly, and Addison hung up without saying whether he was calling it off.

That was Saturday. On Sunday afternoon Kaiya came by with her binder of procedures, and the three of them ended up on the porch with the encyclopedia open between the pitchers of lemonade, arguing about whether the mock parliament had adopted German rules or British ones. Addison had changed his mind about something smaller first: he conceded that a straight vote was lazy. "It's not just power," he said, turning the page. "It's who you hand it to." Kaiya said that was the whole difference between the systems in one sentence, and nobody argued with her. Chase kept his notes in front of him but found himself drafting the other side's argument as carefully as his own, because the truth was he could not tell anymore whether the German rule protected stability or merely made coups more polite. The zeitgeist of their nascent parliament, Kaiya joked, was that nobody trusted anybody yet, and she was right in a way that made him laugh.

His grandmother brought out apple cake and stayed to listen for a while, and his grandfather came out for the last of it and said nothing at all, which Chase understood to mean he had been following the whole thing through the window.

Monday came, and the auditorium's folding seats filled. Mr. Farah-Ali called the session to order, and Addison stood up with his motion. He named the vote of no confidence, and then he named the successor, and it was Kaiya. She looked as surprised as Chase felt, and then she stood too, straightening her binder, and walked to the front to make her case while the clerk counted raised hands.

activity: to interview for a part-time job with confident eye contact and clear answers
knowledge_domain: to interview for a part-time job with confident eye contact and clear answers
fact: Eye-contact norms differ: steady eye contact often signals confidence in North American interviews, while in some East Asian settings prolonged direct gaze at a senior person can seem impolite.
story:
Thomas had two interviews scheduled for Saturday, one at the hardware store and one at the tea shop in the plaza, and his grandmother had strong opinions about both. She sat him at the kitchen table on Thursday night and told him to look the manager straight in the eye the whole time, no blinking, like a man who knows what he wants. His father, home for dinner, disagreed without looking up from his bowl. When Thomas's uncle interviewed people in Seoul, his father said, a young man who stared at a senior that way would seem disrespectful, even aggressive. Thomas said he couldn't do both. His grandmother said he could.

On Friday after last period he found Edmond and Miah in the empty side of the art room, where Ms. Quinn let seniors hang around until the janitor came through. Edmond wanted to use Thomas as a body in his photography project, some series about hands doing nervous things, and he needed three more shots before Monday. Miah already had a job at the tea shop and had gotten it, she admitted, by nodding a lot. Thomas told them the whole problem: steady eye contact meant confidence here, and the same steady gaze at a senior person could read as rude in East Asian settings, and the hardware manager was Mr. Pell, who was from here, and the tea shop was run by a family whose daughter was in Miah's chemistry class.

"So just do both on purpose," Edmond said, adjusting his lens. "Stare at Pell, look politely away from the tea guy."

"That's not a plan, that's two separate plans wearing a trench coat," Miah said.

Edmond took a photograph of Thomas's hands while they argued, and the shutter noise made Thomas flinch, and Edmond said that was exactly the shot he wanted. Thomas tried to verbalize what bothered him, that he didn't want to perform a version of himself that switched depending on who was watching, but it came out as a complaint about trench coats again and Miah laughed so hard Ms. Quinn came in from the hall to see what was happening.

Ms. Quinn asked what the trench coat was. Miah explained, badly, and then Thomas explained it properly, and Ms. Quinn said only that plenty of her students had been coached by relatives from two cultures who gave opposite advice, and that he should probably decide what he actually thought respect looked like. Then she told Edmond to clean the paint sink or she would confiscate the camera, which was not germane to anything but which Edmond obeyed immediately, because Ms. Quinn did not make threats twice.

Thomas walked home and made a list on the back of a chemistry worksheet. Column one: look up, speak clearly, don't mumble. Column two: look up but not fixedly, glance away sometimes, let silences happen. Underneath he wrote "both are just paying attention?" and then crossed out the question mark and left the sentence, which felt like cheating but also felt true. He didn't know whether it was true. That was the part he couldn't resolve, and he was tired of pretending that deciding something made it certain.

At the hardware store on Saturday morning, Mr. Pell asked him where he saw himself in five years, a question so enormous for a job involving shelf-stocking that Thomas almost laughed. He kept his eyes on Pell's face, steady but not locked, and said five years was a long time but he'd be somewhere with a degree and probably a worse commute. Pell wrote something down. At the tea shop in the afternoon, the owner's daughter translated the questions and the owner watched Thomas the whole time. Thomas looked at her when he answered and away when he listened, and once, when she said something in Korean to her daughter that made them both smile, he let himself smile too instead of holding his interview face.

Walking out past the plaza fountain, his phone buzzed twice. The first text was from Edmond: a photo of Thomas's hands on the kitchen table, knuckles pale, the chemistry worksheet half in frame, with the caption "final piece, titled bathos, the giant question and the tiny hands." The second text was from a number he didn't know, and it said, "Can you start Tuesday, 4pm." He stood there for a minute trying to figure out which job it was from the area code. Then Miah came out of the tea shop with her apron folded under her arm and said, "He liked you. He said you listened."

"He said that in English?"

"He said that in a look," Miah said, and pointed at the door. "Go say yes before he changes his mind."

activity: professional tone, structured writing and respectful disagreement in formal communication
knowledge_domain: professional tone, structured writing and respectful disagreement in formal communication
fact: An 'I-message', popularized by psychologist Thomas Gordon, states the speaker's own concern, such as 'I'm worried we'll miss the deadline', instead of accusing the listener with 'you' language.
story:
Joseph had never once left a shift early, and he intended to keep that record spotless, which was why Brock's habit of vanishing at half past four bothered him so much. They volunteered together at the community resource office on Alder Street, answering phones, filing intake forms, stuffing envelopes for the quarterly mailing. The office smelled of toner and old coffee, and Ms. Whitehead, the coordinator, trusted the two of them to close up on Thursdays. Except that on the last three Thursdays, Brock had been out the door before the last phone call was even logged, leaving Joseph to lock the cabinet, run the vacuum, and initial the closing sheet alone.

"He's disenfranchising the whole team," Joseph told Felix at lunch, pleased with the word, which he had picked up in civics that morning. "Some of us take this seriously. My college applications count on it."

Felix pushed his tray an inch away. "You count on it. That's different."

Joseph let that pass, because Felix was doctrinaire about volunteering, forever insisting it should be its own reward, and Joseph had learned not to argue with him on principle. That night, sitting at the kitchen table with the volunteer laptop open, he began drafting a message to Brock. He typed fast, and what came out was fast too: You keep ditching early, you leave everything to me, you obviously don't care about this place at all. He read it back and felt the clean heat of it, the sense of a case closed.

He was still in that reverie, imagining Brock's chastened face, when he went searching the shared drive for the closing-sheet template and found instead a scanned handout someone had left in the wrong folder. It was a page from a communication workshop, and it described something attributed to the psychologist Thomas Gordon. Instead of accusing the listener with "you" language, the page said, state your own concern: something like "I'm worried we'll miss the deadline." Joseph read it twice. He opened his draft again and the word You glared back at him from every line, like a row of pointing fingers.

The next morning he showed the printout to Felix before first period. "It's called an I-message," Felix said, tapping the heading, and Joseph was quietly annoyed that Felix already knew, because Felix had never volunteered anywhere in his life. Still, at lunch they sat with the draft between them and rebuilt it sentence by sentence. Joseph wrote that he was worried they would miss the mailing deadline if the closing tasks fell to one person, that he felt taken for granted on Thursdays, and that he would like to agree on a plan for who locks up which week. It was harder than the angry version, the way carrying a full box is harder than kicking one. He sent it before he could soften it further.

Brock's reply came during sixth period, and Joseph read it under his desk. I'm sorry, it said. I've been leaving early because my mom picks me up at 4:30 for my little brother's dialysis appointments, and I didn't want to make it a whole thing at the office. Ms. Whitehead knows. I should have told you. I can stay late the weeks your mom works nights, if that helps with the vacuum.

Joseph read the last line three times. His mom worked Thursday nights. Someone had been running the vacuum on those evenings, and Joseph tried to remember doing it, and could not clearly, only a memory of the office already dark and clean when he arrived Fridays, which he had somehow filed under his own name. He sat very still while the teacher explained something about supply curves, and the honest thought arrived slowly: he did not actually know whose record was spotless, and probably never had.

After last bell he walked back to the office, the printed I-message folded in his pocket like evidence he wasn't sure was his. Brock was at the front desk, stacking brochures, and Joseph stood in the doorway holding the doorframe the way you do when you haven't decided to come in.

"I'll take the vacuum this Thursday," Joseph said. "And the dialysis weeks, you go. I'll write it down so I remember which is which."

Brock looked up. "You could just ask Ms. Whitehead. She keeps the schedule."

"Yeah," Joseph said. "But I wanted to tell you first."

activity: to compute the integral of a function to find the area under a curve
knowledge_domain: to compute the integral of a function to find the area under a curve
fact: In a definite integral the constant of integration cancels out, because it is added to both F(b) and F(a) and then subtracted away.
story:
Andrew had lost three marks on the last question, and the red circle around his answer was still bothering him two days later, which was why he was standing in the corner store on Delmore Street holding a pop and a pad of graph paper he had no real reason to buy.

Rian was behind the counter, since it was his uncle's store and Rian covered the Thursday shift. He rang up the graph paper without comment, then looked at the pad sticking out of Andrew's backpack. "You still on that test?"

"Four out of ten on the last one," Andrew said. "I did the whole integral right. Wrote the antiderivative, plugged in the numbers. Then I put plus C at the end and she took off marks for it."

Rian leaned on the counter. "For a letter?"

"It was a definite integral," Andrew said. "Bounds and everything. Two to five. I got the right number at the end and she still circled it." He laid the test on the counter, smoothing it flat between the display of lottery tickets and the rack of chips. The final line read: area under the curve equals twelve plus C.

Marianne came in the way she always did after her evening class, shaking rain off her jacket, and stopped when she saw the test. "That's the same thing Rivera got me on last year," she said. "I fought it for a week."

"There's nothing to fight," Rian said. "It's just a rule. No plus C on definite integrals."

"Rules without reasons are just bromides," Marianne said, picking up a chocolate bar. "Rivera says that about the dress code too."

Andrew ignored them both, which was how he handled most of their arguments, and looked at his own work. The antiderivative was F. He had evaluated it at the top bound, five, and written F(5). Then at the bottom bound, two, F(2). Then he had subtracted, F(5) minus F(2), and somewhere in the middle of that his plus C had survived to the last line.

He borrowed Rian's pen from beside the register. On the back of the receipt he wrote it out again, slower. If you add a constant to the antiderivative, then F(5) becomes F(5) plus C. But the same thing happens at the other bound, so F(2) becomes F(2) plus C. He wrote the subtraction with both constants in it, one on each term, and looked at them for a long moment.

"They cancel," he said.

Rian glanced over. "What?"

"The C. You add it at the top and you add it at the bottom, and then you subtract, and it just cancels out. It's not banned. It's pointless." He drew the slash himself, crossing out the plus C in both places, and what remained was the plain number, twelve.

Marianne leaned in to look at the receipt. "So the marks weren't for breaking a rule. They were for carrying something through that was already gone."

"I still think it's a rule," Rian said. A customer came to the counter with milk and a newspaper, and Rian rang it up while Andrew refilled his pen stroke where it had gone thin. The store's cooler hummed. Outside, the rain had slowed to the kind that didn't need an umbrella.

Andrew looked at what he had written and was not fully satisfied, which was its own kind of answer. The arithmetic was clean. The constant appeared on both terms and then disappeared when he subtracted, and he could see it on the paper as plainly as he could see the lottery machine. But he understood, in a way he couldn't yet write down, that he was trusting his own subtraction more than he trusted the notation, and that there was probably a deeper reason, something Rivera would say about families of functions, that he hadn't reached. He had the fact. He didn't have the whole floor under it.

"You going to ask Rivera tomorrow?" Marianne asked, crumbling the wrapper of the chocolate bar she had not paid for yet.

"No point asking about the marks," Andrew said. "She doesn't give them back." He folded the receipt along the line where the two constants cancelled and put it in his pocket with the graph paper. "But I'll ask why. There's got to be more to it than this."

Rian slid the chocolate bar into Marianne's total without telling her, and Andrew watched him do it and said nothing, because some subtractions you let stand. He zipped his backpack, nodded at them both, and pushed out through the door into the wet street, already writing the question in his head.

activity: to plan a weekly training program for a sport with rest days and warm-ups
knowledge_domain: to plan a weekly training program for a sport with rest days and warm-ups
fact: Holding static stretches for a long time, about 60 seconds or more per muscle, right before explosive activity can briefly reduce strength and power, so many programs warm up with dynamic movement.
story:
Emilie spread the binder open across the picnic table at Riverside Park, weighting the corners with her phone and a water bottle because the wind kept lifting the pages. Saturday was circled twice: first race of the season, 100 metres, and above it she had written a week of workouts, Monday through Friday, each day assigned a distance and a pace. Celia leaned over her shoulder, chewing the straw of her drink.

"You've got something written every single day," Celia said.

"That's the problem with it," Emilie said. "Coach said the plan has to include rest. I don't know where rest goes. It feels like a day wasted."

Down on the grass, Linkin was running strides, and beyond him the hillside seemed to undulate in the late light, green rising and falling toward the tree line, so that his figure appeared and disappeared against it. Emilie watched him go. He was the one who had told her, back in the fall, that before his regional final he had sat on the start line and held his long stretches the way he always did, thigh, hamstring, calf, a full minute each, maybe longer, and then felt flat when the gun went off. He'd had nothing in his legs. He came sixth.

"Linkin," she called. He jogged over, breathing hard. "The day you felt flat. How long were you holding those stretches?"

"Like sixty seconds. Maybe more. Everyone does it." He shrugged, took the water bottle, drank. "Why."

"Because I've been putting a stretch routine at the top of every workout page. Ten minutes, hold each one." She flipped the binder around to show him, the neat columns, the minute counts. "I copied it off a plan I found."

Celia pulled the binder closer and squinted at it. "So?"

"So he held stretches for a minute or more right before he raced, and he felt weak." Emilie tapped the page. "I'm doing the same thing before speed days. Before the thing where I need power."

Linkin set the bottle down slowly. "My sprint coach this winter made us do leg swings and walking lunges instead. I thought she just liked making us look stupid."

"Dynamic stuff." Emilie said it half as a question. She pulled out her phone and searched, thumbing past forums, and read for a while, and the page she stopped on said it plainly, that holding a muscle in a long static stretch for about 60 seconds or more, right before explosive activity, can briefly reduce your strength and power, and that was why many training programs warm up with movement instead. She read it twice. She turned the screen toward them without a word.

Celia read it, then looked up at the sky as if the information had come from there. "Huh."

"So everything I wrote for Saturday morning is wrong. It's not just useless, it's working against me." Emilie crossed out the stretch column with two strokes, hard enough to crease the page. Then she sat back. The wind moved the binder again and she pressed it flat with her palm.

Ms. Paquette, who walked the loop path every evening with her terrier, had stopped at the edge of the table and was reading the crossed-out column over Celia's shoulder. Emilie had known her since she was nine, when Ms. Paquette had coached the neighbourhood kids in softball, and she waited now, half expecting a correction.

"Building a plan, are you," Ms. Paquette said. It wasn't really a question. The terrier pulled at the leash toward Linkin's shoes.

"Trying to. It keeps falling apart."

"They all do, the first several. That's how you learn what's in them." She clicked her tongue at the dog and moved on down the path.

Emilie looked at what remained. She moved the long stretches to after the workouts, wrote cool-down beside them, and on the speed days she began listing things she had seen Linkin's coach do, the swings, the lunges, skips, building up to effort. Then, at the top of the week, she left Wednesday blank and wrote REST in smaller letters than she'd written anything else, as though it might still be argued out of existence. Her inchoate plan had at least a shape now, a spine, even if she couldn't yet say whether the rest day was in the right place or whether two speed sessions and a race were too much. There was something like discernment in choosing what to cross out, she thought, more than in anything she'd written in ink in the first place, and she didn't fully trust it.

"Race me to the water fountain," she said to Linkin, closing the binder. "No stretching first. I want to feel the difference."

"You're on," he said, and was already three strides gone.

activity: the language of contracts and forms, such as terms, conditions, liability, consent and signatures
knowledge_domain: the language of contracts and forms, such as terms, conditions, liability, consent and signatures
fact: Under the US Federal Trade Commission's Cooling-Off Rule, buyers can cancel certain sales made at home or at temporary locations until midnight of the third business day after the sale.
story:
Brandon's mother had come home from the wedding expo at the hotel with a folder, and all through dinner the folder sat on the counter like a guest nobody wanted to talk to. It was only after she went to bed that he opened it: a contract for a photography package, eighteen hundred dollars, her signature in blue ink at the bottom of a page dense with terms he didn't recognize. Liability. Indemnification. A clause that said the deposit was nonrefundable under all circumstances. He sat down at the computer in the den with the folder beside the keyboard and typed the first thing he could think of: cancel contract signed at hotel.

The search results loaded with glacial patience, the old router in the den working through its opinion of the world. Somewhere in the fourth page of links he found a government page about sales made at home or at temporary locations like hotel booths. He leaned closer. Under the Federal Trade Commission's Cooling-Off Rule, buyers could cancel certain sales made at home or at temporary locations until midnight of the third business day after the sale. He read the sentence twice, then a third time, mouthing the words. Three business days. The expo had been Saturday. Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, midnight. He checked the clock in the corner of the screen and felt something that was almost exhilaration, a quick bright lift in his chest, because it was Sunday night and the window was still open.

He texted Kohen, who was the kind of person who read terms and conditions for entertainment. Kohen called him within a minute, his voice tinny through the phone propped against a mug. "Hold on, you're telling me she signed it at a booth? At a hotel?"

"That's what the paper says. Temporary sales location, whatever that means."

"It means exactly what you think it means," Kohen said. "Booths, motels, fairgrounds, your living room. Not stores. Stores are different."

"Is there a form? It says the seller was supposed to give her cancellation forms, two copies, at the time of sale." Brandon flipped through the folder again. Photographs of smiling brides, a price sheet, a receipt. No forms. The company had handed over everything except the one document that would let her walk away.

"So they blew it," Kohen said. "But the rule doesn't die because they forgot the paperwork. It's called the Cooling-Off Rule. You should look up how the cancellation itself has to be done, because there's always a way they want it done, and a way that actually counts."

Brandon typed cancellation notice Cooling-Off Rule and found that the notice had to be in writing, dated, signed, and delivered. Delivered how, he wondered, and read until he had an answer that satisfied him: hand delivery, mail, or telegram, a word so soaked in antiquity that he smiled at it, imagining his mother's contract being cancelled by a boy in a cap riding a bicycle. He copied the language of a sample notice into a document and then stopped, cursor blinking, because a question he hadn't earned yet was sitting there: could he sign it for her?

He called Mr. Xu, who lived two doors down and had spent thirty years in insurance before retiring, and who kept his porch light on for no reason Brandon had ever determined. Mr. Xu came to the fence in his cardigan. "It's her signature on the contract," he said when Brandon explained. "So it should be her signature on the cancellation. Yours could raise a question you don't want raised. Consent, Brandon. The whole architecture of a contract is consent. If she didn't consent to the purchase, you can't fix that by not getting her consent to the cancellation."

"That's backwards, though," Brandon said. "She consented to the purchase."

"Did she?" Mr. Xu picked a leaf off the fence and turned it over. "A booth at a wedding expo with a countdown clock and a discount that ends today. That's not consent, that's pressure with a receipt. But the remedy still runs through her hand, not yours. Wake her up."

She was in the kitchen in her robe at six, holding the folder the way people hold things they regret. He told her about the rule, the three business days, the missing forms, and watched her face move from embarrassment to something steadier. "I kept saying I needed to think about it," she said. "And he kept saying the price was only good today. I signed because it was easier than leaving." She read the notice Brandon had drafted, and he brought her his pen from the den, the good one. She dated it, signed it, and then, on her own, added a line requesting written confirmation of the cancellation.

"So I can still mail it tomorrow and be inside the window," she said.

"Hand delivery is cleaner," Brandon said. "We know when it arrives."

What he didn't say, because he was still working it out for himself, was the part he wasn't sure about: whether the rule existed because people like his mother deserved protecting, or because the law had simply decided that some decisions need distance, a cooling interval, the way metal needs to cool before you can tell if the weld holds. Maybe both. Maybe the difference didn't matter at eight in the morning with a signed notice on the table.

They drove to the address on the contract, a strip-mall office with the company logo half peeled from the glass. Inside, a woman at the front desk took the notice in both hands like something fragile. "I'll give this to the owner," she said.

"We'd like something in writing," his mother said, "saying it's cancelled."

The woman looked at the notice, then at the date on it, and reached for a stamp.

activity: to trace the steps of cellular respiration from glucose to ATP in the mitochondria
knowledge_domain: to trace the steps of cellular respiration from glucose to ATP in the mitochondria
fact: The journal Nature rejected Hans Krebs's 1937 paper on the citric acid cycle, and he published it in the journal Enzymologia instead.
story:
The rejection notice was taped to Maximiliano's locker like a wanted poster, though he insisted he'd pinned it there as a joke, and the sardonic grin he wore while saying so convinced nobody. His science fair entry, a table of oxygen-consumption rates in yeast fermenting different sugars, had been knocked back on a formality: one missing signature on the safety sheet, dated wrong, returned with a stencil-stamped paragraph about incomplete documentation. He had spent the whole weekend before the deadline measuring flasks in his garage, and now the regional committee would not even look at his numbers.

"You can resubmit next year," Maelle offered, which was the kind of comfort that made things worse, and Thomas knew it, because the whole point of senior year was that there was no next year that counted.

Thomas had his own reason for hanging around the biology lab after last bell. Mr. Whitaker had posted the unit outline, and the test on cellular respiration sat at the end of it like a wall. Thomas needed to trace the whole route himself, glucose broken down in the cytoplasm, then the fragments shuffled into the mitochondria, where they were dismantled step by step, carbons stripped off as carbon dioxide, and the energy skimmed at each stage into that currency of the cell, ATP. He was not a natural at this. He was, if anything, an unwilling autodidact, someone who taught himself slowly and resentfully, page by page, because listening in class never quite took.

"Sit with me," he told Maximiliano on Wednesday, spreading the diagram on the lab table by the window. "You know this stuff anyway. Yeast, oxygen, sugar. You measured it."

"Measured it for nothing."

"Draw the cycle for me. The citric acid cycle. I keep losing my place." Thomas tapped the diagram, the wheel of reactions turning inside the mitochondrial matrix. "You start with glucose. Glycolysis splits it, that part I have. Then it's like the mitochondria takes over and runs this loop, over and over, siphoning off energy each turn."

Maximiliano drew it, reluctantly, then less reluctantly, arrows and carbons, correcting Thomas where he'd put a step out of order. Somewhere in the third pass Thomas went quiet, and then he started laughing, quietly, at the photocopy he'd pulled from the library that morning. He had gone looking for the man whose name sat in the corner of the diagram, Krebs, and had found the story tucked in the introduction of a thick history of biochemistry.

"Listen to this," Thomas said. "The journal Nature rejected Hans Krebs's 1937 paper on the citric acid cycle."

"Nature," Maximiliano repeated, the way you repeat a curse word to check its weight. "The Nature."

"Rejected it. He published it in the journal Enzymologia instead."

Maelle, who had drifted over from the fume hood, looked from one of them to the other. "The whole cycle? The one we're being tested on?"

"The one in every textbook," Thomas said. "Turned down first."

He didn't dress it up as a lesson, because it wasn't one, exactly, and he didn't want to be the person who turned a man's rejection into a pep talk. But Maximiliano took the photocopy and read it himself, twice, and something in his shoulders came down half an inch. He photocopied the photocopy and taped that to his locker too, beside the rejection notice, without comment.

The week of the test, Thomas stayed late tracing the pathway on the whiteboard, glucose to pyruvate to acetyl, into the wheel, carbon dioxide out, electrons handed down the chain, ATP made. Mr. Whitaker passed through collecting beakers and watched for a minute. "You've got it," he said, which from Mr. Whitaker was nearly a speech.

The results came Friday, in the empty hallway after the buses. Maelle found Thomas first, holding her phone like something fragile. The regional committee had reinstated Maximiliano's entry; a teacher had called, an appeal had been filed, the signature was ruled sufficient after all. His yeast data would go to the fair.

"And you," she said, and hesitated, because Thomas had submitted nothing, but he had told everyone he'd volunteer at the fair's registration table, and the volunteer list, it turned out, had lost his name. "They said the sheet was full. You can try again next year."

Thomas stood there with Krebs's cycle still fresh in his head, the wheel that turned and turned, and Maximiliano came down the hall waving his reinstatement letter, grinning, and called out, "Rejected twice, accepted once. You want to sign my form as a witness?"
